children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.
The leaks also revealed that Cyberglobes collaborated with NSO and salespeople from both companies suggested the products as a package deal.

The system was intended to collect information from mobile devices and could access communications and other data.

Pegasus was subsequently used by Panama's National Security Council to monitor more than 150 people, according to records cited in the U.S. extradition case against former president Ricardo Martinelli. Targets reportedly included political opponents, journalists, judges, business competitors, and at least two U.S. citizens, as well as U.S. Embassy personnel. Investigators recovered Pegasus data including phone calls, WhatsApp and BlackBerry communications, emails, and other personal information.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text:
AccessData Group was a U.S.-based cybersecurity company that developed digital forensics investigation technology. The company created the Forensic Toolkit (FTK), which became an industry-standard tool for extracting and analyzing data from digital devices. The technology was used by law enforcement agencies worldwide, including in Nigeria, where it was employed alongside other forensic tools for extracting information from seized devices.

AccessData's merger with Exterro created a powerful surveillance conglomerate. Their combined digital forensics and data extraction capabilities give law enforcement and government agencies unprecedented access to personal information, particularly given the company's two-decade history of developing tools that can crack passwords, decrypt files, and extract sensitive personal data from devices without user consent.

AccessData's Forensic Toolkit (FTK) was also used by Botswana's Police Service Digital Forensics Laboratory alongside Cellebrite's UFED to conduct invasive searches of journalists' devices. The technology was deployed in the case of Oratile Dikologang, a digital editor, where police "successfully extracted" and "thoroughly analyzed" thousands of messages, contacts, images, audio files, videos, and social media accounts from his phone. When contacted by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) about this surveillance activity, AccessData and its parent company Exterro declined to respond to questions about their technology's use in Botswana's press freedom violations.

RCS Lab has offshoots in France, Germany and Spain, as well as another concealed subsidiary, Azienda Informatica Italiana, which builds interception software for Android and iPhone devices.

children.text: Acxiom is a data broker and marketing technology company headquartered in Conway, Arkansas. Known for its extensive data collection and analytics capabilities, Acxiom aggregates and processes vast amounts of personal information, including demographic details, purchasing behavior, online activity, real-time location, and more. This data is used to create detailed consumer profiles, which are then sold to a wide range of clients, including advertisers, marketers, financial institutions, government agencies and political organizations. In the U.S, the company has held contracts with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the State Department and other federal government agencies.

In 2014, Acxiom acquired LiveRamp, integrating its services to enable cross-device tracking and data onboarding, which helps connect online and offline consumer data. This partnership allows Acxiom to extend its data reach, offering even more granular insights into consumer behavior and location data to a broader range of clients. In 2018, Acxiom claimed to have data on over 2.5 billion people in over 62 countries, including 68% of the global online population.

AccessData Group was a U.S.-based cybersecurity company that developed digital forensics investigation technology. The company created the Forensic Toolkit (FTK), which became an industry-standard tool for extracting and analyzing data from digital devices. AccessData's merger with Exterro created a powerful surveillance conglomerate. Their combined digital forensics and data extraction capabilities give law enforcement and government agencies unprecedented access to personal information, particularly given the company's two-decade history of developing tools that can crack passwords, decrypt files, and extract sensitive personal data from devices without user consent.

AccessData's Forensic Toolkit (FTK) was also used by Botswana's Police Service Digital Forensics Laboratory alongside Cellebrite's UFED to conduct invasive searches of journalists' devices. The technology was deployed in the case of Oratile Dikologang, a digital editor, where police "successfully extracted" and "thoroughly analyzed" thousands of messages, contacts, images, audio files, videos, and social media accounts from his phone. When contacted by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) about this surveillance activity, AccessData and its parent company Exterro declined to respond to questions about their technology's use in Botswana's press freedom violations.

children.text: The Falcon system, developed by Semptian, is primarily designed for tracking the location of targeted cellphones rather than intercepting calls or texts. Similar to the Stingray devices used by U.S. law enforcement, Falcon operates within a nearly 1-mile radius and can pinpoint the location of cellphones with high precision, up to 5 meters accuracy. When activated, Falcon emits signals that compel nearby mobile phones and other cellular devices to connect to it, revealing their exact locations. Falcon includes a smaller, pocket-sized device that can be used by agents on foot to track cellphone locations even more precisely, narrowing down to within 1 meter. This technology enables authorities to conduct targeted surveillance and locate specific individuals within urban or densely populated areas.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

It has its origins linked to a secretive Soviet technologies unit that operated under the KGB. According to Wired, the company's roots can be traced back to the Sharashka Marfino, a special prison for engineers and scientists during the Stalin era. In this facility, individuals plucked from various labor camps were coerced into developing technologies, including voice identification systems used for monitoring calls to foreign embassies in Moscow. According to its website, it worked with Saudi's Ministry of Interior to install an audio forensic lab in the Kingdom.

In 2019, Sberbank, the state-controlled financial powerhouse, finalized the acquisition of a 51% stake in STC. Additionally, Digital Horizon, a venture capital and business incubator firm with offices in Moscow and Tel Aviv, also secured a stake in STC.

According to the BIRN (Balkan Investigative Reporting Network) investigation into surveillance systems in Serbia, STC's voice recognition software was procured by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MUP). Serbian intermediary companies, notably AIGO and IntellSec, facilitated the supply to Serbian state institutions.

children.text: Geolitica, formerly known as PredPol, short for "Predictive Policing," is a software company that claims to use historical crime data to predict where crimes are likely to occur. Its surveillance capabilities rely on analyzing past crime reports, including time, location, and type of crime, to generate "hot spots" for law enforcement to monitor. This data-driven approach enabled police departments, such as the LAPD, to direct patrols and resources to specific areas flagged by the system. PredPol however specifically targeted Black and brown neighborhoods in the U.S, and its algorithms created often false and misleading data that intensified surveillance in these communities.

SoundThinking was formerly known as ShotSpotter, Inc until it changed its corporate name in 2023. ShotSpotter, which retained its name as a product after the rebrand, relies on a network of acoustic sensors that monitor urban environments, effectively turning public spaces into zones of constant surveillance. The accuracy of ShotSpotter has been called into question, with reports indicating that the system can misidentify sounds, leading to unnecessary and dangerous police deployments as well as over-policing in various communities. ShotSpotter is linked to more than 100 law enforcement agencies in the U.S.

Another one of their products, CrimeTracer, functions as a police database and search engine, repackaging and sharing vast amounts of data across a range of law enforcement agencies. The company further consolidated its position in the surveillance industry after acquiring Geolitica, the firm behind PredPol, a predictive policing technology criticized for exacerbating racial inequalities by directing police to already heavily surveilled communities. This merger builds on SoundThinking's previous acquisition of HunchLab in 2018 to provide AI-driven analysis and “predictive policing.”

In addition to police departments, SoundThinking also has contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense in the military market and also maintains a partnership with Israeli weapons manufacturer Airobotics.

children.text: Airship AI builds AI-powered surveillance and monitoring systems for government agencies, law enforcement, and border enforcement operations. Headquartered in Redmond, Washington, the company develops tools to aggregate live feeds from cameras, drones, body-worn devices, and acoustic and seismic sensors into centralized platforms that automatically detect, classify, and flag "activity of interest" in real time, feeding intelligence to police, federal agents, and border officials around the world.

Airship's main platform, Acropolis, pulls video and data management into one place and comes in a version built specifically for police use. Its companion device, Outpost AI, is an edge recorder that captures encrypted video, audio, and sensor metadata while running on-board object detection, OCR, and live streaming directly into Airship's law enforcement management system.

The majority of Airship's business comes from U.S. federal contracts, with its surveillance products deployed across the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the Department of Defense, as well as state and local agencies including the Virginia State Police.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

Allot Communications is an Israeli telecommunications firm that develops Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) technology, which enables Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to monitor, throttle, and block internet traffic, including VPNs, social media platforms, and political content.

Multiple investigations have alleged that Allot's surveillance equipment reached Iran despite Israeli export bans. According to a Bloomberg investigation referenced by Haaretz and The Copenhagen Post, Allot sold its NetEnforcer DPI software to the Danish IT firm RanTek A/S in Randers over a five-year period. RanTek allegedly removed the Israeli labels and repackaged the equipment before passing it to an intermediary who resold it to Iran.
Three former Allot employees told Bloomberg the Iranian destination was an "open secret," though Allot denied knowledge or approval, and RanTek's CEO Morten Kolind denied repackaging the products.

entity.name: RanTek

children.text: RanTek A/S is a Danish IT distributor founded in 1999 and headquartered in Randers, reselling networking and security gear from major Western vendors before being absorbed into the Nordic IT group NetNordic in 2019. In December 2011, a Bloomberg investigation revealed that Israeli vendor Allot Communications' "NetEnforcer" deep-packet-inspection equipment had reached Iran in violation of Israeli export law, routed through RanTek as the intermediary distributor.
Allot's contract restricted RanTek to selling inside Denmark, shipments sent to the Danish company had their original labels stripped and were then forwarded on to Iranian end-users.

children.text:
Almenta is a surveillance firm based in Bulgaria and run by Israeli operators, including CEO Ari Covitz. It develops Wi-Fi-based hacking tools, which it showcased at the Milipol homeland security conference. The company offers a product called WiNA-P, which enables a variety of attacks on smartphones by exploiting Wi-Fi networks. These attacks include delivering malware to extract data from apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook, and Skype, as well as phishing capabilities to steal login credentials through fake landing pages. Almenta also advertises an "Account Grabber" feature to identify iCloud or Android accounts by sending deceptive messages to targets.

Alongside WiNA-P, Almenta promotes a product called “Observer,” which offers “worldwide geo location,” as described in a blurb on Milipol’s website. A brochure for “Observer” reveals that, with only a target’s mobile phone number, the device’s location can be pinpointed and displayed on a Google Maps interface.

The company claims its tools can operate from up to 500 meters away and target as many as 50 devices simultaneously. Almenta's technology reportedly relies on tools from other Israeli surveillance firms, such as WiSpear and Jenovice, with costs for such systems starting at $1 million.

children.text: Jenovice Cyber Labs is an Israeli surveillance technology company founded in 2012 by Israeli intelligence veteran Leon Perez and special forces veteran Tal Gleichger. It offers products like Metropolink, a surveillance system capable of monitoring entire cities by tracking devices through Wi-Fi identifiers such as MAC addresses and geolocation. Its other products include Piranha, a compact, fully automatic Wi-Fi interception device that can operate remotely, and Orion, a geolocation tool designed to track and locate devices by leveraging Wi-Fi signals.

In addition to citywide surveillance, Jenovice has developed Prisonlink, a tool for monitoring unauthorized devices in prisons, and Achilles Cloud Interception, a system designed to extract cloud account information from services like iCloud and Google.
The company primarily serves law enforcement, national security agencies, and military intelligence sectors globally.

Despite a ban on Israeli intelligence and defense exports to Bangladesh, Passitora sold spyware to the country's National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC), a branch of the Interior Ministry responsible for monitoring internet and social media. The company has faced scrutiny in the past, including a scandal in Cyprus involving its SpearHead system, which was used to extract private data from people's phones without their knowledge or consent.
Passitora is part of the Intellexa Alliance, a network of companies marketing and selling spyware globally.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: Sandvine was founded in 2001 in Waterloo, Ontario, by a team of ~30 people from PixStream (a Cisco acquisition).

The company developed deep packet inspection (DPI) technology for network traffic management, which is also used for censorship and surveillance purposes. In 2017, San Francisco-based private equity firm Francisco Partners acquired Sandvine and merged it with its U.S.-based holding Procera Networks in a deal valued at approximately $562 million. Procera had separately developed DPI technology that was used for surveillance and censorship in countries with authoritarian regimes.

Following the merger, Sandvine struck deals with several governments, including in Belarus, Egypt, Eritrea, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. By 2023, Egypt alone accounted for $26 million in annual sales, roughly 13% of the company's total revenue. That same year, researchers at Citizen Lab discovered Sandvine's technology had been used in attempts to inject spyware into the iPhone of Ahmed Eltantawy, an Egyptian politician planning to challenge President El-Sisi.

In February 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department added Sandvine to its Entity List for providing Egypt with "mass web-monitoring and censorship" technology used to block news and target political actors and human rights activists. The blacklisting effectively banned Sandvine from obtaining U.S. technology, and major firms including Microsoft, Zoom, and Intel cut ties with the company. Francisco Partners exited its ownership in August 2024
The DOC removed Sandvine from the Entity List in October, 2024, after the company promised to "undergo transformative changes."
The company has since rebranded to AppLogic Networks.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

Its technologies are built around Lattice, an AI-enabled command-and-control platform that integrates data from sensors, cameras, radar, and autonomous systems to detect, identify, and track people, vehicles, and other objects in real time.

Among Anduril's flagship products are its Autonomous Surveillance Towers (ASTs), which combine AI, radar, and electro-optical cameras to provide continuous, autonomous monitoring. The towers can detect people from up to 2.8 kilometers away and automatically identify and track "objects of interest" without constant human oversight. The company has deployed approximately 300 surveillance towers for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and in 2026 was awarded a $363 million contract to deliver more than 200 additional Extended Range Sentry Towers (XRSTs), expanding its AI-powered border surveillance network.

children.text:
Anomaly Six (A6) is a Virginia-based company founded in 2018 by two ex-military intelligence officers. The company claims to have the capability to track approximately 3 billion devices in real time through GPS data collected via smartphone apps. According to a report by The Intercept, their surveillance system operates by gathering location data through partnerships with "thousands" of apps using software development kits (SDKs). The company also claimed to have the capability to unmask and track intelligence agency (CIA and NSA) personnel during a pitch to Zignal Labs, a social media monitoring company.  The company proposed a joint venture with Zignal Labs that would enable the U.S. government to conduct seamless surveillance operations on adversaries. Anomaly Six's capabilities are largely made possible through the advertising industry's data collection practices, underlining the connection between commercial data brokers and surveillance techniques. 

U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM) paid $589,500 to Anomaly Six in September 2020 for a "Commercial Telemetry Feed." The company's co-founder, Brendan Huff, previously managed Defense Department relationships of another U.S surveillance company called Babel Street.

children.text: Babel Street provides tools that analyzes and monitors social media and other online sources for law enforcement and intelligence purposes. Used by U.S Secret Service, it can scrape data from over 25 social media sites, translate over 200 languages, and set up geo-fences with customizable filtering options. The software can also survey sentiment geographically over time and import data to other surveillance platforms like Palantir.

One of its primary AI products, Babel X, is used by the U.S Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to analyze the social media of U.S. citizens, refugees, and asylum seekers. Babel X can link social media posts to individuals' Social Security numbers, location data, and collect a wide range of other identifiers, including IP addresses, employment history, and unique advertising identifiers. CBP also uses Locate X, an add-on that includes smartphone location data, and has access to AdID information. Locate X can zoom into a specific location and display the movements of smartphones in that area. Each phone, represented by a red dot on the map, can be tracked individually. The tool can show the path a specific device has taken, including stops at various locations.

Babel Street's acquisitions include intelligence company Vertical Knowledge in 2024, Rosette, a text analytics platform, in 2022, and Dunami, a social media intelligence company, in 2020. Its board of advisers includes Robert Ashley, ex-director of the Defense Intelligence Agency.

Oosto is an Israeli company formerly known as AnyVision specializing in facial recognition and tracking technologies. AnyVision initially gained notoriety for its controversial use in monitoring the West Bank border and rebranded to Oosto in September 2021 after it faced significant backlash for its unethical business practices. Despite claims from Oosto that issues like racial bias have been mitigated, skepticism remains, particularly as the company pushes into even more contentious areas like behavior recognition.

In September 2020, AnyVision's/Oosto's shareholders partnered with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems Ltd. to form a joint venture named SightX. This new company, equally owned by AnyVision’s shareholders and Rafael, focuses on developing advanced AI-recognition technologies for military use.
In 2025, the company was acquired by Metropolis, which defines itself as an "AI-driven recognition platform that understands, adapts and responds in real time."

While publicly presenting itself as the "world's 4th largest Critical Infrastructure Security Solutions Company", the company was reportedly involved in hack-for-hire activities, including espionage and targeted surveillance. The company served a wide range of clients, including Israeli private detectives Aviram Halevi and Tamir Mor, who alone commissioned surveillance operations on dozens of targets.

Appin has garnered attention for its aggressive legal campaign to suppress reporting about its past activities, most notably forcing Reuters to temporarily remove an investigative article through an Indian court order. The Association of Appin Training Centers, a successor organization, has pursued legal action against multiple media outlets to remove references to Appin's illegal hacking operations, though this effort has faced resistance from organizations like the Electronic Frontier Foundation and DDoSecrets.

The company's influence persists through numerous successor organizations, with former Appin employees establishing and operating their own firms that continue similar surveillance and hacking operations.

children.text: Sandvine was founded in 2001 in Waterloo, Ontario, by a team of ~30 people from PixStream (a Cisco acquisition).

The company developed deep packet inspection (DPI) technology for network traffic management, which is also used for censorship and surveillance purposes. In 2017, San Francisco-based private equity firm Francisco Partners acquired Sandvine and merged it with its U.S.-based holding Procera Networks in a deal valued at approximately $562 million. Procera had separately developed DPI technology that was used for surveillance and censorship in countries with authoritarian regimes.

Following the merger, Sandvine struck deals with several governments, including in Belarus, Egypt, Eritrea, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. By 2023, Egypt alone accounted for $26 million in annual sales, roughly 13% of the company's total revenue. That same year, researchers at Citizen Lab discovered Sandvine's technology had been used in attempts to inject spyware into the iPhone of Ahmed Eltantawy, an Egyptian politician planning to challenge President El-Sisi.

In February 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department added Sandvine to its Entity List for providing Egypt with "mass web-monitoring and censorship" technology used to block news and target political actors and human rights activists. The blacklisting effectively banned Sandvine from obtaining U.S. technology, and major firms including Microsoft, Zoom, and Intel cut ties with the company. Francisco Partners exited its ownership in August 2024
The DOC removed Sandvine from the Entity List in October, 2024, after the company promised to "undergo transformative changes."
The company has since rebranded to AppLogic Networks.

Equifax is one of the three major U.S. consumer credit reporting bureaus. Operating as a data broker, its products provide U.S. immigration authorities and law enforcement with information used to locate people targeted for arrest and deportation. Between 2005 and September 2024, the U.S Department of Homeland Security (DHS) awarded Equifax contracts worth at least $16.1 million, while total U.S. federal government contracts with the company exceeded $365 million during the same period.

ICE uses or has used multiple Equifax databases, mainly through third-party platforms like LexisNexis Accurint and Thomson Reuters CLEAR, to locate people targeted for arrest or deportation. ICE has also specifically paid for access to data from Appriss, a company Equifax owns.

Since early 2021, ICE has used a database called Justice Intelligence (formerly JusticeXchange), a product of Equifax subsidiary and data broker Appriss Insights. This system collects and makes searchable real-time incarceration release data from thousands of U.S. jails and prisons, which ICE uses to learn the release dates of individuals it targets for deportation. The agency accesses Justice Intelligence as an add-on to its LexisNexis Accurint subscription.

children.text: LexisNexis' Accurint product collects a wide range of data from both public and non-public sources and offers them for sale primarily to government agencies and law enforcement. The platform compiles billions of records from sources such as government databases, utility bills, phone records, license plate tracking and medical records. It also integrates analytics tools like link analysis, detailed location mapping, and pattern recognition.

Accurint is widely used by agencies such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for surveillance purposes, including tracking individuals and conducting deportation raids. FOIA records reviewed by the advocacy organization Mijente show that ICE agents performed more than 1.2 million searches in just seven months during 2021, shortly after the agency contracted with LexisNexis for Accurint. CBP has also invested heavily in the platform, awarding LexisNexis a $25.7 million contract through November 2027 for continued access to Accurint's investigative capabilities.

LexisNexis also integrates facial recognition technology into its monitoring tools, enabling law enforcement and government agencies to identify individuals and analyze images as part of their surveillance and data-gathering efforts.
LexisNexis is a wholly owned subsidiary of RELX PLC, a global information and analytics company headquartered in London.

In 2026, 404 Media revealed that ICE plans to pay LexisNexis millions of dollars for continued access to large datasets, which it intends to feed into Palantir's ELITE system. The system combines data from private companies and government sources to help ICE identify people and neighborhoods for enforcement and deportation operations.

children.text: Thomson Reuters, a major information and data provider, has signed at least three contracts with ICE totaling over $46 million specifically for surveillance services, including their CLEAR platform. The database contains over 400 million utility records, including names, addresses, and service details from utility companies, as well as employment, housing, and credit information. This data includes details sourced from Equifax and is updated daily and provides law enforcement with tools to locate individuals.

Thomson Reuters also helps power an app called Mobile Companion, built alongside Motorola Solutions, that lets ICE officers instantly scan a license plate in the field and add it to a database of billions of records showing where that vehicle has been spotted across the country. That vehicle data can then be combined with other personal information such as driver license data, credit header data, marriage records, vehicle ownership, and voter registrations. The app is also capable of predicting where a car may travel in the future and can collect face scans for facial recognition to help identify vehicle owners. The tool is designed for real-time use by ICE officials in the field, functioning similarly to the agency's existing facial recognition apps but focused on gathering information about vehicles.

children.text: Palantir operates one of the largest and most lucrative surveillance systems. This includes tools to monitor social media activities and using metadata to uncover connections between individuals and groups, as well as DMV records, license plate reader data, employment data, arrest records and more, often for intelligence purposes. In 2022, Utimaco was acquired from the previous owner EQT Partners by SGT Capital.
Utimaco's distributor in the United Arab Emirates is Bulwark Technologies, founded by Indian engineer Jose Menacherry.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

It has become a go-to resource for agencies monitoring users across various platforms, including Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. Its federal clients in the U.S. include the FBI and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) children.text: Quadream Ltd was an Israeli company that provided spyware technology primarily to government clients. The company is best known for its spyware marketed under the name “Reign”, which, like NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, reportedly utilises zero-click exploits to hack into target devices. It was founded in 2014 by a group including two former NSO Group employees, Guy Geva, and Nimrod Reznik. In 2017, a company named InReach was established in Cyprus specifically to promote Quadream products, including Reign, outside of Israel. This was arranged in order to bypass Israeli export controls. Many key employees of both InReach and Quadream have previously worked for NSO Group, Verint, and UTX Technologies.

children.text: AU10TIX is an Israeli identity verification firm that processes government IDs and biometric data for some of the world's largest online platforms, including X (formerly Twitter) and TikTok, where uploaded photo IDs and selfies are sent to the company in Israel for biometric matching.

It operates as a subsidiary of ICTS International N.V. and maintains additional offices in New York, London, Singapore, Amsterdam, and other locations. ICTS International is an aviation and border control firm founded in 1982 by former agents of Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence service.

In early March 2026, a wide range of anonymous X users began reporting that their real names were suddenly being mass Googled inside Israel, often shortly after they posted criticism of Israel's genocide in Palestine. Users pointed to Google Trends data filtered to Israel showing spikes in searches for their legal names, and many connected the pattern directly to AU10TIX, since X required even anonymous users to verify their real identities through the firm to access premium features. The fallout reportedly led X to replace AU10TIX with Stripe for identity verification.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

Its Ayonix Public Security (APS) platform was designed for real-time facial detection and recognition using IP camera video, including identifying people in public spaces and generating alerts when a face matches a database. It also developed FaceMatcher, which allows facial images captured with mobile devices to be searched against databases.
Ayonix has marketed its technology primarily to law enforcement, government, and border control agencies.

The entity was formed from the merger of two sister startups, Azimuth and Linchpin Labs, both of which were acquired by L3Harris. Trenchant operates with strictly compartmentalized teams that develop platform-specific tools, including iOS zero-days and spyware.

In 2025, former Trenchant executive Peter Williams was sentenced to seven years and three months in U.S federal prison after pleading guilty to stealing at least eight software trade secrets, including zero-day exploits and hacking tools, from the company over a three-year period beginning in 2022 and selling them to Operation Zero, a Russian zero-day broker, in exchange for millions of dollars in cryptocurrency.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

entity.name: Operation Zero

children.text: Operation Zero is a Russian zero-day exploit brokerage operating under the legal entity Matrix LLC, owned by Sergey Sergeyevich Zelenyuk. The company has openly stated it will only sell exploits to customers in non-NATO countries, including the Russian government and foreign intelligence agencies. Beyond exploit brokering, Operation Zero has also pursued the development of spyware and tools to extract personal data from users of AI applications such as large language models.

Operation Zero came further into the spotlight when it was revealed that Peter Williams, a 39-year-old Australian national and former executive at U.S. defense contractor L3Harris, stole eight classified zero-day exploits from his employer between 2022 and 2025 and sold them to Operation Zero for millions of dollars. Operation Zero then re-sold these stolen tools, originally intended solely for the U.S. government and its allies, to unauthorized users. Williams was sentenced to over seven years in federal prison after pleading guilty.

In February 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Zelenyuk, Operation Zero / Matrix LLC, and several associates, including Azizjon Makhmudovich Mamashoyev and Oleg Vyacheslavovich Kucherov (a suspected member of the Trickbot cybercrime gang), for their role in acquiring and distributing cyber tools.

Zelenyuk also established a UAE-based technology company called STS specifically to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Russian bank accounts and to conduct business with entities in Asia and the Middle East. STS was among the entities sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury in February 2026 alongside Zelenyuk and Operation Zero.

entity.name: Coruna

children.text: Coruna is an iPhone hacking toolkit first identified by security researchers in February 2025. According to mobile security company iVerify and reporting by TechCrunch, the exploit kit is believed to have been created by the hacking and surveillance division of US military contractor L3Harris and developed for use by the US government.

According to Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which named the toolkit, Coruna contains five complete iOS exploit chains leveraging a total of 23 distinct vulnerabilities, targeting iPhones running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1. The kit primarily exploits Apple's WebKit browser framework, enabling "watering hole" attacks that silently compromise a device when a user simply visits a malicious website. The toolkit is estimated to have infected tens of thousands of phones worldwide.

Coruna has also proliferated beyond its original operator. Google tracked its use by a suspected Russian espionage group (UNC6353) in watering hole attacks targeting Ukrainian users, and later by a financially motivated Chinese cybercriminal operation (UNC6691) stealing cryptocurrency. The exact mechanism of proliferation remains unclear, but Google says it points to an active market for "second-hand" zero-day exploits and unscrupulous brokers facilitating the spread of nation-state-grade tools to criminals and foreign intelligence services.

entity.name: Metrea

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

L3Harris is a US defense contractor company. The company’s communication and surveillance products are used by law enforcement agencies for monitoring and intelligence operations. Used by U.S Secret Service, it can scrape data from over 25 social media sites, translate over 200 languages, and set up geo-fences with customizable filtering options. The software can also survey sentiment geographically over time and import data to other surveillance platforms like Palantir.

One of its primary AI products, Babel X, is used by the U.S Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to analyze the social media of U.S. citizens, refugees, and asylum seekers. Babel X can link social media posts to individuals' Social Security numbers, location data, and collect a wide range of other identifiers, including IP addresses, employment history, and unique advertising identifiers. CBP also uses Locate X, an add-on that includes smartphone location data, and has access to AdID information. Locate X can zoom into a specific location and display the movements of smartphones in that area. Each phone, represented by a red dot on the map, can be tracked individually. The tool can show the path a specific device has taken, including stops at various locations.

Babel Street's acquisitions include intelligence company Vertical Knowledge in 2024, Rosette, a text analytics platform, in 2022, and Dunami, a social media intelligence company, in 2020. Its board of advisers includes Robert Ashley, ex-director of the Defense Intelligence Agency.

children.text:
BadBazaar is a mobile spyware tool with variants targeting both Android and iOS devices. It has been linked to Chinese-backed hacking groups, such as APT15. This group is known by various names assigned by different cybersecurity organizations, including Vixen Panda, Ke3chang, Nickel, Playful Taurus, BackdoorDiplomacy, Mirage, GREF, RoyalAPT, Nylon Typhoon, Flea, and Red Vulture. 

BadBazaar has primarily been used to target Uyghur, Tibetan, and Taiwanese individuals, as well as civil society actors who may oppose Chinese state interests.

The spyware is distributed through trojanized apps, including fake versions of popular communication tools like Signal and Telegram, as well as apps tailored to specific communities, such as Uyghur-language Quran apps. Once installed, BadBazaar can collect sensitive data, including call logs, GPS locations, SMS messages, and files. The spyware has also been observed spreading via social media platforms and official app stores.

The Chengdu-based contractor, Sichuan Dianke Network Security Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as UPSEC), was linked to the deployment of this malware.

children.text: DarkNimbus is a cross platform spyware and remote access trojan (RAT) linked to the threat actor Earth Minotaur. First documented in 2025, it has been deployed against Uyghur and Tibetan communities after being delivered through the Moonshine exploit framework, which abuses vulnerabilities in WeChat and Chromium based applications.

Once installed, DarkNimbus enables extensive surveillance by collecting contacts, SMS messages, call logs, browser data, and messaging app conversations, while also tracking device location, recording phone calls, capturing screenshots and photos, transferring files, and executing remote commands.

Security researchers have linked the broader activity of Earth Minotaur and related Chinese state-aligned operators to targeting ethnic minority groups, human rights advocates, and individuals considered politically sensitive by Beijing.

The Balgh (بلغ - meaning "report" in Arabic) platform, launched by Iraq's Ministry of Interior in January 2023, is a digital tool designed to allow citizens to report social media content deemed to "violate public morals" or "undermine social stability." Within just over a month of its launch, the platform received over 96,000 reports, resulting in prosecutions and prison sentences for individuals accused of publishing content deemed critical or offensive, including creators of music and comedy.

children.text: LexisNexis' Accurint product collects a wide range of data from both public and non-public sources and offers them for sale primarily to government agencies and law enforcement. The platform compiles billions of records from sources such as government databases, utility bills, phone records, license plate tracking and medical records. It also integrates analytics tools like link analysis, detailed location mapping, and pattern recognition.

Accurint is widely used by agencies such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for surveillance purposes, including tracking individuals and conducting deportation raids. FOIA records reviewed by the advocacy organization Mijente show that ICE agents performed more than 1.2 million searches in just seven months during 2021, shortly after the agency contracted with LexisNexis for Accurint. CBP has also invested heavily in the platform, awarding LexisNexis a $25.7 million contract through November 2027 for continued access to Accurint's investigative capabilities.

LexisNexis also integrates facial recognition technology into its monitoring tools, enabling law enforcement and government agencies to identify individuals and analyze images as part of their surveillance and data-gathering efforts.
LexisNexis is a wholly owned subsidiary of RELX PLC, a global information and analytics company headquartered in London.

In 2026, 404 Media revealed that ICE plans to pay LexisNexis millions of dollars for continued access to large datasets, which it intends to feed into Palantir's ELITE system. The system combines data from private companies and government sources to help ICE identify people and neighborhoods for enforcement and deportation operations.
