children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: RCS Lab is an Italian company specializing in the development and sale of surveillance and interception technologies. Founded in 1993 and headquartered in Milan, RCS Lab provides a range of services and products to law enforcement and intelligence agencies worldwide. In 2022, Cy4Gate acquired fellow Italian firm RCS Lab, known for its “Hermit” spyware tools. Google and Meta have observed RCS Lab campaigns in Italy, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Mongolia. Tykelab, a company based in Rome and owned by RCS Lab, had been using dozens of phone networks, often on islands in the South Pacific, to send tens of thousands of secret ‘tracking packets’ around the world, targeting people in countries including Italy itself, Greece, North Macedonia, Portugal, Libya, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Malaysia, Iraq and Mali. RCS Lab has offshoots in France, Germany and Spain, as well as another concealed subsidiary, Azienda Informatica Italiana, which builds interception software for Android and iPhone devices.

Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

General Dynamics Corp is a U.S. defense contractor involved in the development and deployment of surveillance technologies used in border enforcement and immigrant monitoring. Between 2005 and 2019, the company was a contractor for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), building a "smart/virtual" border along the U.S.-Mexico. Its Remote Video Surveillance Systems (RVSS), equipped with day and night capable cameras mounted on vehicles, enable near-constant monitoring of border regions, giving authorities unprecedented oversight over the movement of migrants.

General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), the company’s IT and services arm, has expanded this surveillance infrastructure, including modernizing CBP’s tower systems under the Consolidated Tower & Surveillance Equipment (CTSE) program. These towers, deployed across southern border regions such as Arizona (Nogales, Naco, Yuma, and Ajo) and Texas’s Rio Grande Valley, concentrate state surveillance in communities where migrants are most vulnerable. Newer contracts also extend surveillance infrastructure to parts of the northern U.S. border with Canada, where surveillance towers are being installed or upgraded.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.
The leaks also revealed that Cyberglobes collaborated with NSO and salespeople from both companies suggested the products as a package deal.

Protection, with the equipment delivered to the former U.S. Southern Command headquarters in Panama. The system was intended to collect information from mobile devices and could access communications and other data.

Pegasus was subsequently used by Panama's National Security Council to monitor more than 150 people, according to records cited in the U.S. extradition case against former president Ricardo Martinelli. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: Passitora, previously known as WiSpear, is a Cyprus-based company controlled by former Israeli intelligence commander Tal Dilian. It sells advanced surveillance technology to governments worldwide. Despite a ban on Israeli intelligence and defense exports to Bangladesh, Passitora sold spyware to the country's National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC), a branch of the Interior Ministry responsible for monitoring internet and social media. This technology enables interception of calls, texts, and internet traffic.

The company has faced scrutiny in the past, including a scandal in Cyprus involving its SpearHead system, which was used to extract private data from people's phones without their knowledge or consent.
Passitora is part of the Intellexa Alliance, a network of companies marketing and selling spyware globally.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text:
Almenta is a surveillance firm based in Bulgaria and run by Israeli operators, including CEO Ari Covitz. It develops Wi-Fi-based hacking tools, which it showcased at the Milipol homeland security conference. The company offers a product called WiNA-P, which enables a variety of attacks on smartphones by exploiting Wi-Fi networks. These attacks include delivering malware to extract data from apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook, and Skype, as well as phishing capabilities to steal login credentials through fake landing pages. Almenta also advertises an "Account Grabber" feature to identify iCloud or Android accounts by sending deceptive messages to targets.

Alongside WiNA-P, Almenta promotes a product called “Observer,” which offers “worldwide geo location,” as described in a blurb on Milipol’s website. A brochure for “Observer” reveals that, with only a target’s mobile phone number, the device’s location can be pinpointed and displayed on a Google Maps interface.

The company claims its tools can operate from up to 500 meters away and target as many as 50 devices simultaneously. Almenta's technology reportedly relies on tools from other Israeli surveillance firms, such as WiSpear and Jenovice, with costs for such systems starting at $1 million.

children.text: Trovicor originated as part of Siemens' voice and data recording division. This division became part of Nokia Siemens Networks (NSN) in 2007, a joint venture between Siemens and Nokia Oyj. In March 2009, NSN sold the division, known then as Intelligence Solutions, to Perusa Partners Fund. This move was partly to disassociate NSN from the contentious surveillance industry and its extensive human rights violations. Perusa subsequently rebranded the division as Trovicor, while retaining much of the original equipment and workforce from before the sale. Trovicor’s surveillance and interception products have enabled at least one government in the Gulf to spy on and arrest journalists and dissidents. Trovicor also has a partnership with Gamma Group, developer of the notorious FinFisher spyware. In 2009, when the company was part of NSN, Trovicor sol​d surveillance technology to Iran.
The company is now known as Data Fusion.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: Corsight AI is a facial recognition technology company headquartered in Israel with operations worldwide. The company develops facial recognition and surveillance technology powered by what they call "Autonomous AI," which, according to the company, is based on 15 years of neuroscience research and over 250 patents. Their technology is designed to mimic human facial recognition capabilities.

Corsight's technology allegedly identify individuals even when less than 50% of their face is visible. It also provides real-time alerts and video analysis and claims to identify people wearing masks. More recently, it was developing technology to create facial models from DNA.

Israel implemented a mass facial recognition program in the Gaza Strip using Corsight AI's technology. The system was deployed at military checkpoints along major evacuation routes where Palestinians were fleeing southward, creating an extensive database of Palestinian civilians without their knowledge or consent. The technology faced notable accuracy challenges, particularly when processing grainy footage or partially obscured faces. One significant case highlighting these accuracy issues involved Palestinian poet Mosab Abu Toha, who was wrongfully detained at a checkpoint in mid-November while attempting to leave Gaza for Egypt with his family. After being flagged by the system as a wanted person, he was held in detention for two days, during which he endured beating and interrogation, before being released back to Gaza without explanation.

According to Gizmodo, in 2024 Corsight AI introduced a new surveillance system that monitors "sweethearting" (a practice where retail employees give unauthorized discounts to people they know) by analyzing customer-employee interactions, including physical proximity and visit patterns. The technology, which has already been implemented by unnamed clients, tracks whether customers consistently visit the same employees and triggers security alerts for suspicious patterns.

Corsight also announced a partnership with the public school system in Alagoas, a state in Northeastern Brazil, to implement its facial recognition technology in schools. However, the contract raised transparency concerns: while Alagoas had an active agreement with Teltex, a company acting as Corsight's reseller in Brazil, the contract made no mention of Corsight or the facial recognition solution. According to various researchers and critics, this practice violates local laws.

children.text:
Dark Caracal is a sophisticated cyber-espionage operation linked to Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security (GDGS). Discovered in 2018 by researchers from Lookout and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), this campaign has targeted individuals and organizations across 21 countries, including military personnel, journalists, activists, lawyers, and government officials. Dark Caracal employs advanced surveillance tools, such as the custom Android malware "Pallas," which is embedded in trojanized versions of secure messaging apps like WhatsApp, Signal, and Threema. These tools enable the extraction of sensitive data, including messages, call records, photos, and account credentials.

The operation relies on spear-phishing and social engineering tactics to compromise devices, often directing victims to download malware-laden apps through fake links on platforms like Facebook and WhatsApp.

children.text: DarkMatter is now known as CPX. Operating under the codename Project Raven, this cybersecurity firm employed former NSA operatives to conduct hacking and surveillance on behalf of the United Arab Emirates. Their targets included journalists, activists, and political opponents of the UAE government​. Interviews with nine former Raven operatives, along with a review of thousands of pages of project documents and emails, show that surveillance techniques taught by the NSA were central to the UAE’s efforts to monitor opponents. The operatives utilized an arsenal of cyber tools, including a cutting-edge espionage platform known as Karma, in which Raven operatives say they hacked into the iPhones of hundreds of activists and political leaders. DarkMatter was founded in 2014 by Faisal Al Bannai, who also created Axiom, one of the largest sellers of mobile devices in the region.

children.text: WeChat, known as Weixin in China, is a multifunctional messaging app developed by Tencent. children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: Sandvine was founded in 2001 in Waterloo, Ontario, by a team of ~30 people from PixStream (a Cisco acquisition).

The company developed deep packet inspection (DPI) technology for network traffic management, which is also used for censorship and surveillance purposes. In 2017, San Francisco-based private equity firm Francisco Partners acquired Sandvine and merged it with its U.S.-based holding Procera Networks in a deal valued at approximately $562 million. Procera had separately developed DPI technology that was used for surveillance and censorship in countries with authoritarian regimes.

Following the merger, Sandvine struck deals with several governments, including in Belarus, Egypt, Eritrea, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. By 2023, Egypt alone accounted for $26 million in annual sales, roughly 13% of the company's total revenue. That same year, researchers at Citizen Lab discovered Sandvine's technology had been used in attempts to inject spyware into the iPhone of Ahmed Eltantawy, an Egyptian politician planning to challenge President El-Sisi.

In February 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department added Sandvine to its Entity List for providing Egypt with "mass web-monitoring and censorship" technology used to block news and target political actors and human rights activists. The blacklisting effectively banned Sandvine from obtaining U.S. technology, and major firms including Microsoft, Zoom, and Intel cut ties with the company. Francisco Partners exited its ownership in August 2024
The DOC removed Sandvine from the Entity List in October, 2024, after the company promised to "undergo transformative changes."
The company has since rebranded to AppLogic Networks.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.

In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.

children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

children.text: Palantir operates one of the largest and most lucrative surveillance systems. This includes tools to monitor social media activities and using metadata to uncover connections between individuals and groups, as well as DMV records, license plate reader data, employment data, arrest records and more, often for intelligence purposes. It works with entities such as the U.S army on AI-powered targeting systems, and is also known to supply surveillance products to Israel through strategic partnerships.

In April 2025, 404 Media revealed that the U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has paid Palantir tens of millions of dollars to expand its database and search tool, enabling "complete target analysis of known populations" and updating enforcement priorities. This collaboration supports technical infrastructure tied to controversial and racially targeted mass deportation efforts.

Palantir also built the Maven platform, which the U.S. military calls its "AI-powered battlefield platform." Maven collects and analyzes surveillance data from "war zones" to speed up U.S. military operations, including lethal airstrikes. The platform aggregates information from satellites, spy planes, drones, intercepted telecommunications, and the internet, packaging it into a searchable app for commanders.

In January 2026, 404 Media reported that Palantir has developed a tool for ICE called "ELITE" that creates a map populated with potential deportation targets. The system provides detailed dossiers on individuals and assigns a "confidence score" to each person's current address. ICE uses this tool to identify locations where multiple people it might detain are based, effectively helping the agency plan neighborhood raids.

In 2026, records revealed that ICE plans to pay LexisNexis millions of dollars for continued access to large datasets, which it intends to feed into Palantir's ELITE system. The system combines data from private companies and government sources to help ICE identify people and neighborhoods for enforcement and deportation operations.

children.text: Dataminr is a New York–based artificial intelligence company that scans social media and other publicly available data in real time to generate alerts, and its tools are widely used to facilitate government and law enforcement monitoring. The company was an early recipient of funding from In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture capital arm, which invests in technologies with intelligence gathering applications.

In March 2024, it was revealed that Elon Musk's X, then known as Twitter, was selling user data to Dataminr. In 2020, The Intercept reported that police used Dataminr to surveil George Floyd protests; documents later showed the company sent Washington, D.C. police over 160,000 alerts about planned protests between 2020 and 2022, and in 2022 it alerted the U.S. Marshals Service to the times and locations of pending abortion rights demonstrations.
In May 2025, police records obtained by The Intercept revealed that Dataminr was used by the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) to monitor pro-Palestine protests and related public demonstrations.

Dataminr's own product materials also described a use case in which its Geospatial Analysis application was used during a student demonstration at the University of Cape Town in South Africa to monitor protest hashtags and location specific keywords.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

name: DCHSpy

children.text: DCHSpy is an Android spyware program linked to the Iranian state-aligned cyber-espionage group known as MuddyWater (which is believed to operate under Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security). It has been observed being distributed by disguising itself as seemingly legitimate apps, such as fake VPN clients like Earth VPN and Comodo VPN, as well as variants using Starlink branding, to trick users into installing it.

Once installed, DCHSpy can harvest a wide range of sensitive data from the compromised device, including WhatsApp data, SMS messages, contact lists, call logs, files, precise location, audio recordings, and photos by accessing the microphone and camera. It also compresses and encrypts the stolen information and sends it to attacker-controlled servers.

The spyware has been detected targeting users, particularly activists, journalists, and dissidents, via links shared over messaging platforms like Telegram. Research shows that newer strains of DCHSpy have specifically added the ability to exfiltrate WhatsApp data, targeting users who rely on encrypted messaging to communicate.

children.text: Corsight AI is a facial recognition technology company headquartered in Israel with operations worldwide. The company develops facial recognition and surveillance technology powered by what they call "Autonomous AI," which, according to the company, is based on 15 years of neuroscience research and over 250 patents. Their technology is designed to mimic human facial recognition capabilities.

Corsight's technology allegedly identify individuals even when less than 50% of their face is visible. It also provides real-time alerts and video analysis and claims to identify people wearing masks. More recently, it was developing technology to create facial models from DNA.

Israel implemented a mass facial recognition program in the Gaza Strip using Corsight AI's technology. The system was deployed at military checkpoints along major evacuation routes where Palestinians were fleeing southward, creating an extensive database of Palestinian civilians without their knowledge or consent. The technology faced notable accuracy challenges, particularly when processing grainy footage or partially obscured faces. One significant case highlighting these accuracy issues involved Palestinian poet Mosab Abu Toha, who was wrongfully detained at a checkpoint in mid-November while attempting to leave Gaza for Egypt with his family. After being flagged by the system as a wanted person, he was held in detention for two days, during which he endured beating and interrogation, before being released back to Gaza without explanation.

According to Gizmodo, in 2024 Corsight AI introduced a new surveillance system that monitors "sweethearting" (a practice where retail employees give unauthorized discounts to people they know) by analyzing customer-employee interactions, including physical proximity and visit patterns. The technology, which has already been implemented by unnamed clients, tracks whether customers consistently visit the same employees and triggers security alerts for suspicious patterns.

Corsight also announced a partnership with the public school system in Alagoas, a state in Northeastern Brazil, to implement its facial recognition technology in schools. However, the contract raised transparency concerns: while Alagoas had an active agreement with Teltex, a company acting as Corsight's reseller in Brazil, the contract made no mention of Corsight or the facial recognition solution. According to various researchers and critics, this practice violates local laws.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Dreamlab Technologies, a Swiss company, was involved in a surveillance project in Turkmenistan in partnership with Gamma International GmbH (creators of the FinFisher spyware). Documents leaked by WikiLeaks revealed that Dreamlab helped establish an "Infection Proxy Infrastructure" on Turkmenistan's networks, enabling widespread surveillance. This infrastructure allowed for the infection of devices through fake software updates, file downloads, or website injections, granting full access to personal data, emails, social media messages, and even enabling remote control of microphones and cameras. Dreamlab provided technical services, including network analysis, hardware and software installation, staff training, and system maintenance. The leaked documents suggest the two companies also collaborated for similar interception projects in Oman.

According to Intelligence Online, Dreamlab has since diversified its operations, creating new ventures like Slinf, a threat intelligence firm co-founded with German SIGINT experts, which develops tools such as RATspotting for detecting command-and-control servers and CyKnife for open-source intelligence. Dreamlab previously collaborated with German defense group Rheinmetall to create the consulting firm Cyel. In 2019, Cyel was split, with part of its operations integrated into Dreamlab and the rest taken over by Rheinmetall under the name Cyber Works.
Dreamlab maintains offices in Switzerland, Germany, Spain, Oman, Malaysia, Australia, New Zealand, Bolivia, Peru, India, Malaysia and Chile.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text: Root Networks (RN) is an Israeli company that developed systems capable of infiltrating local area networks (LANs) and intercepting communications without requiring cooperation from telecom operators. This capability enables intelligence services to conduct long-term surveillance and execute Man-in-the-Middle attacks to access encrypted communications. Captured data is redirected via VPN tunnels for detailed analysis.

RN's technology exploits vulnerabilities in router firmware to gain remote access. By mapping and infiltrating vulnerable routers, the company establishes its own interception network, independent of traditional operators. This network allows RN to monitor target devices, such as smartphones and computers, and deploy spyware for further surveillance.

Root Networks was founded by Avi Yarim, a former Rayzone Group specialist, and was led by CTO Shahar Mor, an ex-cybersecurity researcher at Verint. The company shares investors with Rayzone Group, including prominent figures like Yohai Ben-Zakai, a former deputy commander of Unit 8200, and businessman Eran Reshef.

children.text: Fink Telecom Services is a Swiss telecommunications company that has been providing infrastructure that allows surveillance firms and governments to track mobile phone users and intercept private communications worldwide.

The company exploits loopholes in the SS7 signaling protocol, an older mobile network communication standard, by supplying surveillance firms with the ability to "ping" mobile networks as if they were legitimate mobile providers. This capability enables clients to track the real-time location of phone users, redirect SMS messages to crack into internet accounts protected by two-factor authentication, intercept millions of sensitive security codes and logins from major services including Google, Meta, Amazon, WhatsApp, Viber, Signal, banks, crypto exchanges, and dating sites.
Fink has put their surveillance capability at the disposal of governments and private companies globally, including Israel's Rayzone Group, a spyware company.

children.text: Rayzone offers a suite of tools for interception, data extraction, and location tracking. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

entity.name: Operation Zero

children.text: Operation Zero is a Russian zero-day exploit brokerage operating under the legal entity Matrix LLC, owned by Sergey Sergeyevich Zelenyuk. The company has openly stated it will only sell exploits to customers in non-NATO countries, including the Russian government and foreign intelligence agencies. Beyond exploit brokering, Operation Zero has also pursued the development of spyware and tools to extract personal data from users of AI applications such as large language models.

Operation Zero came further into the spotlight when it was revealed that Peter Williams, a 39-year-old Australian national and former executive at U.S. defense contractor L3Harris, stole eight classified zero-day exploits from his employer between 2022 and 2025 and sold them to Operation Zero for millions of dollars. Operation Zero then re-sold these stolen tools, originally intended solely for the U.S. government and its allies, to unauthorized users. Williams was sentenced to over seven years in federal prison after pleading guilty.

In February 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Zelenyuk, Operation Zero / Matrix LLC, and several associates, including Azizjon Makhmudovich Mamashoyev and Oleg Vyacheslavovich Kucherov (a suspected member of the Trickbot cybercrime gang), for their role in acquiring and distributing cyber tools.

Zelenyuk also established a UAE-based technology company called STS specifically to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Russian bank accounts and to conduct business with entities in Asia and the Middle East. STS was among the entities sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury in February 2026 alongside Zelenyuk and Operation Zero.
