entity.name: Coruna

children.text: Coruna is an iPhone hacking toolkit first identified by security researchers in February 2025. According to mobile security company iVerify and reporting by TechCrunch, the exploit kit is believed to have been created by the hacking and surveillance division of US military contractor L3Harris and developed for use by the US government.

According to Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which named the toolkit, Coruna contains five complete iOS exploit chains leveraging a total of 23 distinct vulnerabilities, targeting iPhones running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1. The kit primarily exploits Apple's WebKit browser framework, enabling "watering hole" attacks that silently compromise a device when a user simply visits a malicious website. The toolkit is estimated to have infected tens of thousands of phones worldwide.

Coruna has also proliferated beyond its original operator. Google tracked its use by a suspected Russian espionage group (UNC6353) in watering hole attacks targeting Ukrainian users, and later by a financially motivated Chinese cybercriminal operation (UNC6691) stealing cryptocurrency. The exact mechanism of proliferation remains unclear, but Google says it points to an active market for "second-hand" zero-day exploits and unscrupulous brokers facilitating the spread of nation-state-grade tools to criminals and foreign intelligence services.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: Palantir operates one of the largest and most lucrative surveillance systems. This includes tools to monitor social media activities and using metadata to uncover connections between individuals and groups, as well as DMV records, license plate reader data, employment data, arrest records and more, often for intelligence purposes. It works with entities such as the U.S army on AI-powered targeting systems, and is also known to supply surveillance products to Israel through strategic partnerships.

In April 2025, 404 Media revealed that the U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has paid Palantir tens of millions of dollars to expand its database and search tool, enabling "complete target analysis of known populations" and updating enforcement priorities. This collaboration supports technical infrastructure tied to controversial and racially targeted mass deportation efforts.

Palantir also built the Maven platform, which the U.S. military calls its "AI-powered battlefield platform." Maven collects and analyzes surveillance data from "war zones" to speed up U.S. military operations, including lethal airstrikes. The platform aggregates information from satellites, spy planes, drones, intercepted telecommunications, and the internet, packaging it into a searchable app for commanders.

In January 2026, 404 Media reported that Palantir has developed a tool for ICE called "ELITE" that creates a map populated with potential deportation targets. The system provides detailed dossiers on individuals and assigns a "confidence score" to each person's current address. ICE uses this tool to identify locations where multiple people it might detain are based, effectively helping the agency plan neighborhood raids.

In 2026, records revealed that ICE plans to pay LexisNexis millions of dollars for continued access to large datasets, which it intends to feed into Palantir's ELITE system. The system combines data from private companies and government sources to help ICE identify people and neighborhoods for enforcement and deportation operations.

children.text: Mobile Companion is a field-ready app used by the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers that functions as a real-time vehicle surveillance tool. Powered by Motorola Solutions and Thomson Reuters, the app allows officers to instantly scan a license plate and cross-reference it against a database containing billions of records, revealing where that vehicle has been spotted across the U.S. The app can also predict where a car may travel in the future.

Beyond vehicle tracking, Mobile Companion aggregates a wide range of personal data, including driver license records, credit header data, marriage records, vehicle ownership, and voter registrations, allowing officers to quickly build a profile on a vehicle's owner. The app can also collect face scans for facial recognition purposes. It is designed to operate similarly to ICE's existing facial recognition apps but is specifically focused on gathering intelligence about vehicles and their owners.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.
The leaks also revealed that Cyberglobes collaborated with NSO and salespeople from both companies suggested the products as a package deal.

children.text: M.L.M. Protection Ltd. is an Israeli security company that served as the intermediary for Panama's purchase of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware. In 2012, Panama's National Security Council contracted to acquire Pegasus for $13.4 million through M.L.M. Protection, with the equipment delivered to the former U.S. Southern Command headquarters in Panama. The system was intended to collect information from mobile devices and could access communications and other data.

Pegasus was subsequently used by Panama's National Security Council to monitor more than 150 people, according to records cited in the U.S. extradition case against former president Ricardo Martinelli. Targets reportedly included political opponents, journalists, judges, business competitors, and at least two U.S. citizens, as well as U.S. Embassy personnel. Investigators recovered Pegasus data including phone calls, WhatsApp and BlackBerry communications, emails, and other personal information.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

According to Google researchers, Lipizzan is a multi-stage spyware capable of monitoring and extracting a user’s emails, SMS messages, location data, voice calls, and media files. children.text: Toka is an Israeli company launched in 2018 as a "one-stop hacking shop for governments," developing tools that give law enforcement, intelligence, and military clients the ability to remotely hack into any internet-connected device, beyond smartphones, specifically targeting Internet of Things (IoT) devices like Amazon Echos, Google Nest products, connected fridges, thermostats, alarms, and security cameras.

The company was co-founded by former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak, retired IDF Brigadier General Yaron Rosen (former Chief of the IDF's cyber staff and lead architect of all IDF cyber activities, including those of Unit 8200), Alon Kantor (former VP of Business Development at Check Point Software, a firm founded by Unit 8200 veterans), and Kfir Waldman (former CEO of Go Arc and former Director of Engineering at Cisco).

As of December 2024, the company has raised $37.5 million and works exclusively with governments, including U.S. agencies, militaries, and law enforcement. Toka is expanding its U.S. operations, hiring roles like a "Client Director USA" to grow its business with the Department of Defense and national security agencies. The company recruited Mike Stahala, a former FBI attaché in Ankara, Turkey, for its Washington, D.C. office.

Countries known to have engaged Toka include Nigeria, Ghana, Moldova, and Chile. Specifically, they are confirmed as recipients of Toka's defensive "Cyber Designers" cybersecurity advisory services, funded through the World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank. Israeli media has reported these development bank partnerships were planned by a Netanyahu-era inter-ministerial committee aimed at advancing Israel's political interests in the developing world.

children.text: Avnon Group is an Israeli firm that develops and distributes surveillance technologies through various subsidiaries, such as Bler and Tactic Lab. It's founded by Tomer Avnon, a former Israeli Navy SEAL.

The company offers various tools for intelligence and law enforcement, like IMSI catchers and Wi-Fi sniffing equipment, to enable real-time mobile tracking and wireless communication interception. According to its official website, it operates in over 80 countries worldwide.

The company also has a significant relationship with Egypt, where its subsidiary Bler sold its monitoring tools, specifically its Webint Center platform, to Egypt's Technical Research Department through intermediaries.
Avnon sold social media-tracking software to Hungary, allowing the government to monitor online discourse and public opinion. The sale was approved by Israel's Defense Ministry.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

Examity is an online exam proctoring service contracted by universities and other institutions to monitor students during remote tests. It operates using students' own laptops, tablets, and phones to observe them during exams.

To register for an exam, students must hand over a photo ID, full name, email, phone number, and a biometric template of their typing rhythm. Once the exam begins, a live proctor, often based overseas, asks the test taker to share their screen, display both sides of a driver's license to the webcam, and slowly rotate the camera 360 degrees to scan their workspace. The student is then typically required to hand over remote access to their own computer, which often includes having to enter their system password while the proctor watches.

For the duration of the test, the proctor stares at the student's face looking for "suspicious" behavior and flags incidents that can later be sent to the instructor. Examity's own policy says it may collect names, addresses, biometric records, driver's license numbers, and passwords, and that it can share that data with third parties.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: PenLink is a software company that develops communications surveillance and data analysis solutions for law enforcement. It has become a go-to resource for agencies monitoring users across various platforms, including Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. Its federal clients in the U.S. include the FBI and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) PenLink's flagship products, PLX and PenPoint, enable law enforcement to collect and analyze large amounts of data, including social media interactions and telecommunications records.

In 2022, PenLink acquired GeoTime, which develops data collection and analysis software, and in 2023, it acquired the Israeli surveillance company Cobwebs Technologies, which develops software that aggregates data from phones and social media, converting it into intelligence.

In October 2025, The Washington Post reported that PenLink supplied ICE with Weblocs, a cellphone location tracking system that allows the agency to monitor individuals’ movements without obtaining a court warrant.

In April 2026, the Citizen Lab published an in-depth analysis of Webloc, describing it as a global geolocation surveillance system that monitors hundreds of millions of people using data purchased from consumer apps and digital advertising. The report revealed that Webloc's customers extend well beyond ICE to include the U.S. military, multiple local police departments, and foreign governments, including Hungarian domestic intelligence and El Salvador's national police. The Citizen Lab also found that Cobwebs Technologies founder Omri Timianker, who now oversees PenLink's international operations, has links to the spyware vendor Quadream.
Review the Surveillance Watch entry for Cobwebs Technologies for more information and countries of deployment.

children.text: Tangles is a surveillance tool developed by Cobwebs Technologies, which was founded in Israel by former members of Israeli military special units. It was acquired by PenLink in 2023 and is now available via PenLink's portal of surveillance products.

Tangles operates as an AI-driven web platform that gathers data from the open, deep, and dark web. Its notable feature, WebLoc, allows clients to track the movements of mobile devices within a designated virtual area using geofencing, all without the need for a search warrant or subpoena.

children.text: Ataka Enterprise PTE Ltd is a Singapore based surveillance technology reseller with regional offices in Indonesia, Hong Kong, and Bahrain, serving as a key distribution channel for Israeli spyware vendor Wintego Systems and other international surveillance companies.

An Amnesty International Security Lab investigation discovered a blog post by a self identified Ataka employee, published in April 2019, explicitly naming the Indonesian National Police as a partner to whom Ataka supplies "the Helios Android and Tactical Web Intelligence" system.

Wintego's Helios spyware (distinct from Intellexa's product of the same name) is classified by Amnesty International as a form of highly invasive spyware capable of remotely compromising Android devices and intercepting communications including WhatsApp messages.

Archived versions of Ataka's website indicate the company distributed surveillance products from multiple international vendors, including: FLIR, PenLink (specifically Tangles), Voyager Labs, and Cobwebs Technologies.

children.text: Cobwebs Technologies is an Israeli company whose surveillance software collects data from phones and social media activity. Cobwebs also developed Lynx, a tool for managing fake online identities, and Trapdoor, a social engineering platform that the Citizen Lab assesses can help facilitate the deployment of malware.
Cobwebs founder Omri Timianker has links to the spyware vendor Quadream and now oversees Penlink's international operations.

The three Cobwebs founders have since taken over key executive roles at Penlink. Cobwebs' Israeli, U.K., and German entities were rebranded under the Penlink name.

U.S. customers of Webloc and Tangles include ICE, the U.S. military, Texas Department of Public Safety, DHS West Virginia, NYC district attorneys, and police departments in Los Angeles, Dallas, Baltimore, Tucson, Durham, and smaller jurisdictions. International users include Hungarian domestic intelligence (since at least 2022) and the national police in El Salvador.

children.text: STAR Inteligencia & Tecnología (STAR) is a Colombian surveillance technology company that developed and assembled Esperanza, Colombia’s nationwide fixed line and mobile communications interception platform. According to Privacy International, STAR integrated its own interception hardware and software with technologies supplied by US and British companies including PenLink and Komcept Solutions.
Esperanza could intercept mobile and fixed line call data and content and was administered by Colombia’s Fiscalía General de la Nación, with access provided to other law enforcement agencies.

STAR also built its own interception system, Octopus. According to Privacy International, it collects phone, internet and lawful-interception traffic and forwards it to police monitoring centres. Beyond Esperanza, STAR supplied interception equipment, data-analysis platforms and command centres, and distributed products for several foreign surveillance firms.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: Quadream Ltd was an Israeli company that provided spyware technology primarily to government clients. The company is best known for its spyware marketed under the name “Reign”, which, like NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, reportedly utilises zero-click exploits to hack into target devices. It was founded in 2014 by a group including two former NSO Group employees, Guy Geva, and Nimrod Reznik. In 2017, a company named InReach was established in Cyprus specifically to promote Quadream products, including Reign, outside of Israel. This was arranged in order to bypass Israeli export controls. Many key employees of both InReach and Quadream have previously worked for NSO Group, Verint, and UTX Technologies.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: Wave Guard Technologies is an Israeli surveillance technology company that develops AI-assisted cellular intelligence and geolocation systems for government, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Its core platform, Tracer, analyzes cellular network metadata to locate and monitor mobile devices, track voice calls, SMS, data sessions, and other network events, and reconstruct historical movement patterns for investigations. The company markets Tracer as a nationwide "mass geolocation" platform capable of monitoring border areas.
The company also offers Titan, which provides the collection, analysis, and user deanonymization of Telegram users and data, and Artemis, an IMSI catcher platform.

AdVantage, an advertising intelligence (AdINT) platform. In a 2026 investigation, Le Monde identified Wave Guard as one of several companies marketing AdINT tools capable of using smartphone advertising identifiers and location data to track devices. During confidential presentations attended by Le Monde, company representatives claimed they could deanonymize advertising data by correlating it with other datasets to identify individuals, while Wave Guard promoted its capabilities with the slogan, "Any device, anytime, anywhere."

Investigative reporting from El Faro found procurement documents showing the police acquired or sought to acquire the Wave Guard Tracer system through Israeli reseller EyeTech Solutions. The platform was marketed for real-time and historical mobile phone geolocation, communication analysis, and movement tracking.
A 2020 Haaretz investigation reported that Wave Guard's mobile tracking technology had been marketed and sold to law enforcement agencies in Latin America through Israeli intermediaries.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

Founded in 2014 by former Mossad member Doron Cohen, Fifth Dimension became a leading producer of surveillance technology with the backing of notable figures such as former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz, who served as the company's chairman, and former Mossad deputy head Ram Ben-Barak. children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

children.text: PCS Security Pte Ltd (PCSS) is a Singaporean surveillance and security systems integrator that has been in operation since 1998 and is a supplier of government surveillance infrastructures in Singapore as well as internationally. Marketing materials from the company note that it has been playing a "vital role in Singapore's homeland security" for more than 25 years by entering into a Strategic Partnership for Innovation (SPI) agreement with HTX, the Singapore government agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs that develops technologies for public safety and homeland security operations.

According to the leaked WikiLeaks documents, the company was one of the clients of FinFisher, a German surveillance software provider that exploits vulnerabilities in commonly used software applications like iTunes and Microsoft Word to take control over the devices and obtain information. According to reports, PCS Security is alleged to have paid approximately €3.2 million for the use of FinFisher's spyware that works across all major operating systems including Windows, OS X, Linux, and Android.

The company also offers training on Magnet Forensics, which is a digital investigation tool that is used to extract and analyze data from computers and mobile phones, often used by government agencies for digital surveillance and data collection.
The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

children.text: Fink Telecom Services is a Swiss telecommunications company that has been providing infrastructure that allows surveillance firms and governments to track mobile phone users and intercept private communications worldwide.

The company exploits loopholes in the SS7 signaling protocol, an older mobile network communication standard, by supplying surveillance firms with the ability to "ping" mobile networks as if they were legitimate mobile providers. children.text: Root Networks (RN) is an Israeli company that developed systems capable of infiltrating local area networks (LANs) and intercepting communications without requiring cooperation from telecom operators. This capability enables intelligence services to conduct long-term surveillance and execute Man-in-the-Middle attacks to access encrypted communications. Captured data is redirected via VPN tunnels for detailed analysis.

RN's technology exploits vulnerabilities in router firmware to gain remote access. By mapping and infiltrating vulnerable routers, the company establishes its own interception network, independent of traditional operators. This network allows RN to monitor target devices, such as smartphones and computers, and deploy spyware for further surveillance.

Root Networks was founded by Avi Yarim, a former Rayzone Group specialist, and was led by CTO Shahar Mor, an ex-cybersecurity researcher at Verint. The company shares investors with Rayzone Group, including prominent figures like Yohai Ben-Zakai, a former deputy commander of Unit 8200, and businessman Eran Reshef.

children.text: Rayzone offers a suite of tools for interception, data extraction, and location tracking. One of its products, Geomatrix, is a surveillance software that enables real-time geolocation of mobile devices. It can track phones across 2G, 3G, and 4G networks by using phone numbers or IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) numbers. The platform also supports the creation of geofences, virtual boundaries that trigger alerts when a device enters or exits specified areas. This capability allows for precise monitoring and tracking of individuals.

Another tool offered by Rayzone, called Echo, is marketed by the company as a "Platform for Location Investigations." It's designed to locate an individual, or a group of people, on a geographical basis, pinpointing a target's position and movement path with an accuracy of up to one meter, while also extracting additional information from applications installed on the target's device.

First WAP's surveillance technology has been used across more than 160 countries, tracking over 14,000 unique phone numbers. The company marketed its products to authoritarian governments and made them accessible to corporate actors through a network of middlemen. Fivecast is a company that develops AI-powered software used by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to analyze online content for potential threats. Utilizing artificial intelligence, Fivecast's software detects sentiment and emotion in social media posts and recognizes objects in images and videos. It also scans for "risk terms and phrases" across multiple languages, gathering data from both major social platforms like Facebook and Reddit, as well as smaller communities like 4chan and Gab. 

CBP has spent millions on Fivecast's technology, which they use to monitor individuals they believe may pose risks to public safety, national security, or lawful trade and travel. Fivecast's tools are capable of mapping out networks of connections and tracking persons-of-interest starting with minimal information, as demonstrated in their promotional materials.

Fivecast is headquartered in Adelaide, Australia. The company was co-founded in 2017 by Brenton Cooper, Duane Rivett, Ross Buglak, and David Blockow. Fivecast has a strong connection to the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which includes agencies from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. The company's tools have been developed in consultation with law enforcement and intelligence agencies from these Five Eyes nations, optimizing their software to meet the specific requirements of these agencies for monitoring and analyzing online threats.

children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text:
Fog Data Science, a data broker, sells location data about individuals to law enforcement agencies, obtained from thousands of apps on Android and iOS app stores. The company's web application, Fog Reveal, provides detailed histories of people's lives, selling access for less than $10,000 per year. In the U.S alone, Fog has past or ongoing contractual relationships with at least 18 local, state, and federal law enforcement clients. Fog's service allows for "pattern of life" analyses, revealing an individual's daily routines and habits. The service can execute broad searches, such as gathering device IDs for everyone in a specific area.

The company also uses a "Project Intake Form" that requests detailed information about persons of interest, including their medical provider locations, and harvests location data from smartphones through apps and advertising systems. Critics, including former law enforcement officials, have expressed alarm over the tool’s ability to track individuals in private spaces, such as homes, without judicial oversight.

The company was founded in 2016 by two former Department of Homeland Security officials, Robert Liscouski and Matthew Broderick, who served under President George W. Bush.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

Founded in 2014 by former Mossad member Doron Cohen, Fifth Dimension became a leading producer of surveillance technology with the backing of notable figures such as former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz, who served as the company's chairman, and former Mossad deputy head Ram Ben-Barak. The company's systems are employed to analyze large amounts of data, including social media activity, to identify potential security threats and prevent incidents before they occur. Fifth Dimension collaborated with the Israel Police on a project involving artificial intelligence for law enforcement purposes. This partnership, which did not go through a tender process, involved a pilot program costing about 4 million shekels ($1.1 million) and concluded in 2017. The initiative was described as a "game changer" by Police Chief Roni Alsheikh. However, Fifth Dimension ceased operations due to U.S. sanctions on one of its investors, Viktor Vekselberg, which affected its primary market in the U.S.

The company ceased operations in December 2018, after an unsuccessful acquisition bid from NSO Group. At its height, Fifth Dimension had secured $40 million in funding and employed 100 people.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.
The leaks also revealed that Cyberglobes collaborated with NSO and salespeople from both companies suggested the products as a package deal.

Protection, with the equipment delivered to the former U.S. Southern Command headquarters in Panama. The system was intended to collect information from mobile devices and could access communications and other data.

Pegasus was subsequently used by Panama's National Security Council to monitor more than 150 people, according to records cited in the U.S. extradition case against former president Ricardo Martinelli. Targets reportedly included political opponents, journalists, judges, business competitors, and at least two U.S. citizens, as well as U.S. Embassy personnel. Investigators recovered Pegasus data including phone calls, WhatsApp and BlackBerry communications, emails, and other personal information.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Ability is a security firm based in Tel Aviv. The company develops and provides interception and decryption communication tools to security and intelligence agencies, military forces, police and homeland security services.

Its surveillance capabilities include both passive and active interception of cellular communications across GSM, CDMA, UMTS, and LTE networks, as well as satellite communication interception for systems like Thuraya, Iridium, and VSAT. Ability also offers decryption tools to break encrypted communications and geolocation technologies for tracking cellular devices, and developed the Crosscan system, a portable IMSI catcher for tracking mobile devices. Its operations span across 50 countries worldwide.
Ability cooperated with NSO Group on Pegasus and handled the network side of NSO’s operations.

children.text: DSSL (Digital Security Systems Lab) is a Russian developer and supplier of video surveillance and security systems. children.text: The Chinese government uses Hikvision's AI-enabled technology for mass surveillance and racial profiling. Beginning in 2016, authorities installed tens of thousands of Hikvision surveillance cameras in Ürümqi to monitor every movement of the Uyghur population in East Turkistan (renamed Xinjiang by China). The company was found to have received at least $275 million in government contracts to build surveillance in the region and has developed AI cameras that can detect physical features of Uyghur ethnicity. With over 600,000 Hikvision networks, the United States has the second-highest number of the company’s cameras, followed by Vietnam. In 2019, the US passed a bill banning Hikvision from holding any contracts with the federal government.

A Reuters report revealed that Myanmar's military junta installed Chinese-built facial recognition cameras in key urban centers to strengthen its surveillance capabilities, with technology provided by Hikvision alongside other Chinese surveillance giants, Zhejiang Dahua Technology and Huawei Technologies Co Ltd.
Hikvision is one of China's largest exporters of surveillance cameras and facial recognition tools.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text: Eagle Commercial is a Colombian technology company that has been documented as a local partner and contractor in the country's communications interception infrastructure. The company worked with Israeli surveillance technology provider NICE Systems on the expansion of Colombia's PUMA interception platform, a system operated by Colombian authorities to intercept telecommunications. According to reporting cited by Privacy International, Eagle Commercial was NICE's Colombian partner in contracts involving the system, including an expansion funded by the Colombian government in 2007.

A 2025 Amnesty International investigation found that between 2019 and 2023, US company Axon shipped roughly US$8 million of goods to Eagle Commercial across 194 shipments, with the equipment including several models of TASER.
It reports cases of TASER use involving alleged human-rights violations and says deployment of TASERs had been observed during the policing of public assemblies.

children.text: Gaggle is a Dallas, Texas based company that provides ongoing AI-powered surveillance in schools. children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

FinFisher has been used by various governments and law enforcement agencies around the world for surveillance purposes. The software is designed to monitor and intercept communications, gather intelligence, and track individuals' activities. FinFisher is known for its comprehensive surveillance capabilities, which include: remote access, data extraction of information such as emails, SMS, files, and browser history, real-time monitoring of communications and online activities, keylogging to capture passwords and other sensitive information, microphone and camera activiation to record audio and video, as well as geolocation tracking. Gamma Group dissolved its FinFisher unit in 2014, but several German companies have since sold the spyware.

children.text: PCS Security Pte Ltd (PCSS) is a Singaporean surveillance and security systems integrator that has been in operation since 1998 and is a supplier of government surveillance infrastructures in Singapore as well as internationally. Marketing materials from the company note that it has been playing a "vital role in Singapore's homeland security" for more than 25 years by entering into a Strategic Partnership for Innovation (SPI) agreement with HTX, the Singapore government agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs that develops technologies for public safety and homeland security operations.

According to the leaked WikiLeaks documents, the company was one of the clients of FinFisher, a German surveillance software provider that exploits vulnerabilities in commonly used software applications like iTunes and Microsoft Word to take control over the devices and obtain information. According to reports, PCS Security is alleged to have paid approximately €3.2 million for the use of FinFisher's spyware that works across all major operating systems including Windows, OS X, Linux, and Android.

The company also offers training on Magnet Forensics, which is a digital investigation tool that is used to extract and analyze data from computers and mobile phones, often used by government agencies for digital surveillance and data collection.
The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

children.text: PCS Security Pte Ltd (PCSS) is a Singaporean surveillance and security systems integrator that has been in operation since 1998 and is a supplier of government surveillance infrastructures in Singapore as well as internationally. Marketing materials from the company note that it has been playing a "vital role in Singapore's homeland security" for more than 25 years by entering into a Strategic Partnership for Innovation (SPI) agreement with HTX, the Singapore government agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs that develops technologies for public safety and homeland security operations.

The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text:
Geedge Networks is a Chinese cybersecurity firm that helped build China’s "Great Firewall" and now sells a commercialized version of that system abroad. Founded in 2018, the company’s Tiangou Secure Gateway can filter websites and apps, conduct real-time surveillance, throttle or shut down entire regions of the internet, pinpoint anonymous users, and automatically block circumvention tools such as VPNs and Tor.

Leaked internal files show Geedge exporting these capabilities to authoritarian clients, including Kazakhstan, Ethiopia, Myanmar and Pakistan. In Pakistan, Geedge tech replaced Sandvine equipment in 2023 to create “WMS 2.0,” the country’s upgraded national firewall. 

Engineers at Geedge actively reverse-engineer popular privacy tools, listing commercial VPNs as “resolved” problems and rolling out blockers like the Psiphon detector deployed after Myanmar’s 2021 coup.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

term.name: ALPR
term.definition: Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras are automated surveillance systems that use cameras and software to automatically capture, analyze, and store vehicle license plate information from passing vehicles. These systems record not only license plate numbers but also associated data including the vehicle's location, date, time, make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, creating searchable databases.

children.text: ) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.
