children.text:
BI Incorporated is a subsidiary of the GEO Group, a private prison company that operates more than a dozen for-profit immigrant detention centers nationwide on behalf of ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) in the United States. BI Incorporated operates the technology and manages the system for the U.S. government's Alternatives to Detention program. This program uses various surveillance tools to monitor migrants and asylum seekers awaiting their immigration proceedings. The surveillance technologies used in the Alternatives to Detention program include GPS-enabled ankle monitors, voice recognition technology, and a mobile app called SmartLINK that uses facial recognition software and geolocation for check-ins. The program's surveillance creates "digital enclaves" - areas with high concentrations of monitored migrants, effectively extending the border's reach into various U.S. cities and neighborhoods. 

According to The Guardian, BI Incorporated runs the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program (ISAP), a surveillance system launched in 2004 and marketed as a way to keep immigrants out of detention centers while they await court hearings on their legal status. The program is highly lucrative: the U.S. government pays BI hundreds of millions of dollars a year to operate ISAP, and in 2020 the company signed a five-year contract with ICE worth nearly $2.2 billion.

The company is expanding its surveillance toolkit. In April, 2023, ICE announced it was pilot testing a facial recognition smartwatch as a potential addition to their e-monitoring systems. That device, marketed as VeriWatch, is a non-removable, smartwatch / wrist tracker that combines ongoing GPS location monitoring with biometric facial matching and two-way messaging, replicating the surveillance functions of a traditional ankle monitor. In 2025, it was revealed that ICE intends to expand its surveillance program by fitting over 180,000 immigrants with ankle monitors (and wrist trackers for pregnant women) while they await court proceedings. These devices are supplied and managed by BI Incorporated.

children.text: Geolitica, formerly known as PredPol, short for "Predictive Policing," is a software company that claims to use historical crime data to predict where crimes are likely to occur. Its surveillance capabilities rely on analyzing past crime reports, including time, location, and type of crime, to generate "hot spots" for law enforcement to monitor. This data-driven approach enabled police departments, such as the LAPD, to direct patrols and resources to specific areas flagged by the system. PredPol however specifically targeted Black and brown neighborhoods in the U.S, and its algorithms created often false and misleading data that intensified surveillance in these communities.

Another one of their products, CrimeTracer, functions as a police database and search engine, repackaging and sharing vast amounts of data across a range of law enforcement agencies. The company further consolidated its position in the surveillance industry after acquiring Geolitica, the firm behind PredPol, a predictive policing technology criticized for exacerbating racial inequalities by directing police to already heavily surveilled communities. This merger builds on SoundThinking's previous acquisition of HunchLab in 2018 to provide AI-driven analysis and “predictive policing.”

In addition to police departments, SoundThinking also has contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense in the military market and also maintains a partnership with Israeli weapons manufacturer Airobotics.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

Gloo, a data analytics company, uses digital surveillance to benefit churches and evangelical campaigns. The company mines personal online data, often belonging to vulnerable populations like immigrants or those facing personal crises, to enable churches to target individuals.

Gloo has been linked to campaigns like the $1 billion "He Gets Us" initiative, which uses targeted advertising to promote Christian messages. Although "He Gets Us" initially denied selling data to Gloo, evidence showed that Gloo used data from their campaigns to sell contact information of individuals seeking spiritual support to churches.

Through Gloo's Explorer program, the personal data of individuals responding to "He Gets Us" social media ads was sold to local pastors or anyone willing to pay $49/month. This included sensitive information, such as contact details, without proper vetting or guidelines on how the data should be used. In one incident, a pastor publicly shared private messages from a person and exposed her identity to everyone in her church after she responded to an ad on Instagram.

children.text: Gravy Analytics is a company that provides location intelligence and data analytics services. It's the parent company of Venntel, which sells smartphone location data, including to U.S. government agencies. It provides detailed location data that can help law enforcement agencies understand patterns of movement and behavior in specific areas. In 2023, Gravy Analyrics merged with Unacast, a company that uses machine learning and artificial intelligence to provide location intelligence products.

In January 2024, hackers claim to have breached the company. The hackers allege they have stolen sensitive data such as customer lists, industry information, and precise location data from smartphones, threatening to release it publicly.

children.text: Grayshift, an American company best known for its tools to unlock encrypted mobile devices, has reportedly supplied its technology to Belarusian authorities to hack into locked mobile devices, aiding the Belarusian government in its extensive surveillance operations. These measures include real-time video monitoring systems and direct access to communications data.
Its GrayKey product is a forensic access tool that enables the extraction of encrypted or inaccessible data from mobile devices, including those protected by alphanumeric passcodes.

In 2023, Grayshift merged with Magnet Forensics, a Canadian digital forensics company, to create a combined entity focused on providing advanced digital investigation tools to law enforcement and public safety agencies.

children.text: PCS Security Pte Ltd (PCSS) is a Singaporean surveillance and security systems integrator that has been in operation since 1998 and is a supplier of government surveillance infrastructures in Singapore as well as internationally. Marketing materials from the company note that it has been playing a "vital role in Singapore's homeland security" for more than 25 years by entering into a Strategic Partnership for Innovation (SPI) agreement with HTX, the Singapore government agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs that develops technologies for public safety and homeland security operations.

According to the leaked WikiLeaks documents, the company was one of the clients of FinFisher, a German surveillance software provider that exploits vulnerabilities in commonly used software applications like iTunes and Microsoft Word to take control over the devices and obtain information. According to reports, PCS Security is alleged to have paid approximately €3.2 million for the use of FinFisher's spyware that works across all major operating systems including Windows, OS X, Linux, and Android.

The company also offers training on Magnet Forensics, which is a digital investigation tool that is used to extract and analyze data from computers and mobile phones, often used by government agencies for digital surveillance and data collection.
The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: MSAB is a Swedish forensic technology company. Its software, XRY, which can decrypt passwords and recover deleted data, was reportedly used by Hong Kong police in 2020 to access pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong's phone in under an hour.  Leaked documents in 2021 showed that Myanmar's military junta used MSAB's technology to extract data from phones, including deleted content. In the U.S, the San Diego Police Department employs MSAB's XRY software to extract data from mobile devices in investigations. It's also used by the FBI and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB), among other government agencies.

MSAB developed tools for CPB to gather information from vehicles at border crossings by extracting data from car infotainment systems. These systems store a wealth of information, including call logs, text messages, GPS locations, and paired device data.
MSAB's phone extraction tools were also supplied to Moroccan authorities under EU-funded border management programs to surveil migrants transiting North Africa.
Its reseller in Hong Kong is S-Tech, which also sells surveillance tools from Oxygen Forensics and BlackBag (acquired by Cellebrite in 2020.)

children.text: Oxygen Software, a Russia-based company, develops mobile forensics tools marketed under its U.S branch, Oxygen Forensics. These tools are primarily deployed by government agencies and are widely used for surveillance purposes. Their capabilities include extracting vast amounts of data from mobile devices, such as personal messages, call logs, location data, and other sensitive information. Governments, particularly in Central Asia, such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, have reportedly used them to monitor activists, journalists, and political dissidents. In the U.S, its tools are used by the U.S Army, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), alongside other government agencies. According to an investigation by Gizmodo, U.S. school districts are also amongst its users. For example, Cypress-Fairbanks ISD in Texas confirmed using Oxygen Forensics' tools to extract data from students' phones for "evidentiary purposes."

Oxygen Forensics' tools have also been supplied to Morocco as part of an EU funded program. According to an investigation by Disclose, Oxygen Forensics provided the Moroccan police with a data extraction and analysis system called "Detective," which can bypass locked phone screens to retrieve information stored on cloud computing platforms managed by Google, Microsoft, and Apple, as well as hack supposedly secure applications on any mobile phone or computer.
Oxygen Software’s tools are often sold through regional resellers, such as Softline, which has offices in Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

In September 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the arrests of Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Davydov on allegations that they concealed the company’s Russian ownership and the fact that its software was developed in Russia while obtaining contracts from U.S. government agencies.

children.text: Griaule is a Brazilian biometric technology company that supplies governments, police and military organizations with systems for facial, fingerprint, iris and palm print identification. Its Griaule Biometric Suite (GBS) is designed to manage large biometric databases and perform automated searches for investigators. The company says its investigation platform can match fingerprints, palm prints, faces and irises against databases, identify people during police encounters, and process hours of footage from multiple CCTV cameras for facial recognition.

Griaule also markets a dedicated real-time facial recognition system and mobile biometric identification technology. Its government customers include Brazil's Federal Police and state public security agencies. The company says its technology has also been deployed by Mexican law enforcement and prison systems.

Griaule says the U.S. Department of Defense began using its biometric identification technology in 2018 for operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, including for border control purposes. Its technology is also used in Arizona by law enforcement agencies.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text:
Founded in 2014 by former Mossad member Doron Cohen, Fifth Dimension became a leading producer of surveillance technology with the backing of notable figures such as former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz, who served as the company's chairman, and former Mossad deputy head Ram Ben-Barak. The company's systems are employed to analyze large amounts of data, including social media activity, to identify potential security threats and prevent incidents before they occur. The company specializes in predictive policing tools and comprehensive data analysis, including sophisticated data processing techniques to identify patterns and correlations based on mass surveillance data. 

Fifth Dimension collaborated with the Israel Police on a project involving artificial intelligence for law enforcement purposes. This partnership, which did not go through a tender process, involved a pilot program costing about 4 million shekels ($1.1 million) and concluded in 2017. The initiative was described as a "game changer" by Police Chief Roni Alsheikh. children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: Tykelab, a little-known company based in Rome, has been utilizing dozens of phone networks, often located on remote Pacific islands, to send tens of thousands of secret “tracking packets” worldwide. These packets target individuals in countries such as Libya, Nicaragua, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Iraq, Mali, Greece, and Portugal, as well as within Italy itself. Tykelab exploits longstanding but often unaddressed vulnerabilities in global phone networks, allowing third parties to track phone users’ locations and potentially intercept their calls without leaving any trace on the devices. Tykelab’s parent company, RCS Lab, has also developed a powerful phone hacking tool called Hermit. Once installed on a victim’s device, Hermit can remotely activate the phone’s microphone, record calls, access messages, call logs, contacts, photos, and other sensitive data.

children.text: Advanced German Technology (AGT) is a surveillance vendor founded by two Syrian-German brothers, Anas and Aghiath Chbib. While it has a letterbox office in Berlin, Germany, its operational headquarters is in Dubai, UAE.

AGT is a provider of various surveillance technologies, offering a suite of products that includes interception, digital forensics, and social media monitoring. The company claims to serve corporations, governments, law enforcement, and intelligence agencies worldwide.

According to a Privacy International investigation, AGT enabled the construction of surveillance systems in Syria over a decade leading up to the Arab Spring. Between 2007-2012, AGT partnered with Italian-headquartered RCS to propose using US-origin equipment for a satellite internet monitoring project aimed at intercepting communications. Documents also reveal that AGT was prepared to sell probes from US firm AccessData to MTN Syria, one of the country's mobile service providers, despite US sanctions restricting such exports at the time.
Additionally, AGT was involved in surveillance operations in Libya under Muammar Gaddafi's regime.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: Altron was a Kharkiv based Ukrainian technology company that supplied communications monitoring and tracking equipment. Its products included hardware for recording digital, analog, and IP telephone calls, as well as GPS based vehicle tracking systems. Documents published through WikiLeaks identified the company as providing technology for analyzing telephone calls and internet communications, with listed customers including Ukraine’s Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Defense, and Security Service (SBU).

Altron also acted as an intermediary between Belarusian law enforcement and Hacking Team, facilitating Belarusian interest in Hacking Team's spyware. In 2011 and 2012, Altron employees communicated with Hacking Team about demonstrating or selling the spyware to Belarusian authorities
OCCRP reported that Belarusian law enforcement sought Hacking Team spyware through Altron, although no sale was confirmed.

children.text: Providence Group provides surveillance, intelligence, tactical surveillance equipment, and offensive cyber capabilities to government and law enforcement customers. Its corporate network included Providence Australasia, Providence UK, Providence BNLX, and Providence Inc.
The company acted as an intermediary for surveillance technologies including Hacking Team's remote access spyware and the Kailax Windows Unlocker.

An internal Hacking Team email stated that Providence was representing "the Special Forces from Defence" in Australia in discussions concerning spyware. Separately, Providence Australasia supplied multimedia surveillance equipment to Australia's Department of Defence, while Australian Federal Police records show that the agency purchased cameras from Providence Australasia.
The Dutch National Police acknowledged purchasing products and services for police or detection activities, although the specific products were withheld.

ABC reported that Providence facilitated an opportunity with Ecuador's Ministry of Interior. The proposed customer was described as a newly formed group serving several policing agencies, tasked with monitoring social networks.

entity.name: Robotec

children.text: Robotec Colombia is a Colombian technology company that served as an intermediary and distributor for Italian spyware vendor Hacking Team in Latin America. Leaked Hacking Team documents show that Robotec brokered sales of Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS/Galileo) to government agencies in Colombia, Ecuador, and Panama. In Colombia, the National Police acknowledged a contractual relationship with Robotec for Hacking Team's spyware. Investigative reporting indicate the police acquired Galileo and contacted Hacking Team directly to activate the system.

In Ecuador, Robotec acted as an intermediary in the sale of Hacking Team's surveillance system to the National Intelligence Secretariat (SENAIN). The package included licenses for monitoring computers and mobile devices, with Robotec providing local support and training in Quito.
In Panama, Robotec Colombia brokered the 2011 sale of Hacking Team's Galileo to the Office of Security of the Presidency, with a Robotec subsidiary established in the country.

children.text: TAMCE (Tecnología Avanzada en Medidas y Contramedidas Electrónicas) is an intelligence technology company with operations in Mexico and across Latin America. The company supplies surveillance equipment and services for law enforcement, military, intelligence agencies, and other government bodies, including GPS tracking, telecommunications intelligence, IMSI catchers, forensic extraction tools, and OSINT products.

Leaked Hacking Team emails show TAMCE CEO Nicolás Ruggiero communicating directly with Hacking Team representatives from 2014 and 2015 about business opportunities in Argentina and Latin America. In 2015, Ruggiero sought to arrange presentations of Hacking Team's RCS to Argentina’s intelligence and security agencies and reported meeting former AFI director Oscar Parrilli. A 2026 SocialTIC investigation lists TAMCE as a probable local distributor for Hacking Team, and as the confirmed local distributor of IMSI catchers from Phoenix Worldwide Industries.
The company is registered in Argentina as TAMCE S.R.L. and as TAMCE Contramedidas S.A. de C.V. in Mexico.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: Palantir operates one of the largest and most lucrative surveillance systems. This includes tools to monitor social media activities and using metadata to uncover connections between individuals and groups, as well as DMV records, license plate reader data, employment data, arrest records and more, often for intelligence purposes. It works with entities such as the U.S army on AI-powered targeting systems, and is also known to supply surveillance products to Israel through strategic partnerships.

In April 2025, 404 Media revealed that the U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has paid Palantir tens of millions of dollars to expand its database and search tool, enabling "complete target analysis of known populations" and updating enforcement priorities. This collaboration supports technical infrastructure tied to controversial and racially targeted mass deportation efforts.

Palantir also built the Maven platform, which the U.S. military calls its "AI-powered battlefield platform." Maven collects and analyzes surveillance data from "war zones" to speed up U.S. military operations, including lethal airstrikes. The platform aggregates information from satellites, spy planes, drones, intercepted telecommunications, and the internet, packaging it into a searchable app for commanders.

In January 2026, 404 Media reported that Palantir has developed a tool for ICE called "ELITE" that creates a map populated with potential deportation targets. The system provides detailed dossiers on individuals and assigns a "confidence score" to each person's current address. ICE uses this tool to identify locations where multiple people it might detain are based, effectively helping the agency plan neighborhood raids.

In 2026, records revealed that ICE plans to pay LexisNexis millions of dollars for continued access to large datasets, which it intends to feed into Palantir's ELITE system. The system combines data from private companies and government sources to help ICE identify people and neighborhoods for enforcement and deportation operations.

children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: The Falcon system, developed by Semptian, is primarily designed for tracking the location of targeted cellphones rather than intercepting calls or texts. Similar to the Stingray devices used by U.S. law enforcement, Falcon operates within a nearly 1-mile radius and can pinpoint the location of cellphones with high precision, up to 5 meters accuracy. When activated, Falcon emits signals that compel nearby mobile phones and other cellular devices to connect to it, revealing their exact locations. Falcon includes a smaller, pocket-sized device that can be used by agents on foot to track cellphone locations even more precisely, narrowing down to within 1 meter. This technology enables authorities to conduct targeted surveillance and locate specific individuals within urban or densely populated areas.

children.text:
Semptian, a Chinese company, manufactures surveillance tools used by authoritarian governments across the Middle East and North Africa. These tools, including the Aegis system, Owlet, Falcon, and HawkEye, enable extensive monitoring of citizens' digital activities and communications. Its technologies are also capable of intercepting emails, such as Gmail (through a tool called Gmail Retriever), and analyzing vast amounts of data for surveillance purposes. They also develop GSM geo-location tools and the POMS (Public Opinion Monitoring System) platform for social media monitoring. 

Semptian collaborates with American companies like IBM and Xilinx to enhance its surveillance capabilities, despite concerns over human rights abuses in the regions where its technology is deployed. The company's devices intercept phone calls, texts, and internet usage.

Headquartered in Shenzhen, the company is led by its founder Chen Longsen, also known as George Chen, who previously served as the director of the local branch of the American cryptography and computer security company SafeNet.

children.text: The HawkEye device, developed by Semptian and sold to governments, is a portable surveillance platform that integrates advanced facial recognition technology. It is designed to be deployed in various locations to establish what the company calls a "temporary surveillance scene." HawkEye operates by scanning individuals as they pass by its camera, capturing images of their faces in real time. These images are then compared against extensive databases containing millions of photographs. If a match is found with a person of interest or a suspect in the database, HawkEye triggers an alert, notifying authorities immediately.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Israeli firm Candiru was founded in 2014 by Eran Shorer and Yaakov Weizman. It is thought to be Israel’s second-largest spyware maker after NSO Group. With funding from NSO investors as well as the government of Qatar, its systems have been found to have been operated by multiple countries, including Saudi Arabia, Israel, UAE, Hungary, Indonesia, and Uzbekistan. In November 2021, the US Commerce Department added Candiru and NSO to its trade blacklist.

According to Haaretz, the largest shareholder in Isaac Zack, who has been its chairman since the beginning and was also a founding funder of NSO. In 2021, malware manufactured by Candiru was found on the phones of politicians, journalists, and scholars in Iran, Yemen, Israel, the United Kingdom, and Turkey. Candiru has changed names multiple times, to Grindavik, then DF Associates, then Taveta, then Saito Tech, but it is still commonly known as Candiru. 

Researchers from Recorded Future's Insikt Group have identified active infrastructure associated with Candiru's spyware, known as DevilsTongue, in Hungary and Saudi Arabia. This spyware targets Windows systems and is believed to be deployed through spear-phishing emails, malicious links, and compromised websites.

In 2025, Integrity Partners, a U.S. investment firm, acquired Candiru’s assets for up to $30 million, moving its operations and staff to the new entity Integrity Labs Ltd., which is not subject to U.S. sanctions. The deal aims to bypass U.S. restrictions after Candiru was blacklisted in 2021 over national security concerns.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: Equus Technologies is an Israeli company behind an advanced spyware, known as "Lipizzan," designed to steal users' data. The company offers custom solutions for law enforcement, intelligence agencies, and national security organizations. According to Google researchers, Lipizzan is a multi-stage spyware capable of monitoring and extracting a user’s emails, SMS messages, location data, voice calls, and media files. Google identified 20 Lipizzan apps, which were distributed in a highly targeted manner to fewer than 100 devices. In response, Google has blocked both the developers and the apps from the Android ecosystem. Besides malware, the source reported that Equus Technologies also offers app and cloud interception technology packaged as portable devices. These devices, which can be carried in backpacks, are designed to connect to nearby cellphones and steal passwords along with other sensitive personal data. At least one employee of Equus Technologies is a former staff member of NSO Group, the notorious Israeli malware vendor.

children.text:
Founded in 2014 by former Mossad member Doron Cohen, Fifth Dimension became a leading producer of surveillance technology with the backing of notable figures such as former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz, who served as the company's chairman, and former Mossad deputy head Ram Ben-Barak. The company's systems are employed to analyze large amounts of data, including social media activity, to identify potential security threats and prevent incidents before they occur. The company specializes in predictive policing tools and comprehensive data analysis, including sophisticated data processing techniques to identify patterns and correlations based on mass surveillance data. 

Fifth Dimension collaborated with the Israel Police on a project involving artificial intelligence for law enforcement purposes. This partnership, which did not go through a tender process, involved a pilot program costing about 4 million shekels ($1.1 million) and concluded in 2017. The initiative was described as a "game changer" by Police Chief Roni Alsheikh. However, Fifth Dimension ceased operations due to U.S. sanctions on one of its investors, Viktor Vekselberg, which affected its primary market in the U.S.

The company ceased operations in December 2018, after an unsuccessful acquisition bid from NSO Group. At its height, Fifth Dimension had secured $40 million in funding and employed 100 people.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.
The leaks also revealed that Cyberglobes collaborated with NSO and salespeople from both companies suggested the products as a package deal.

Protection, with the equipment delivered to the former U.S. Southern Command headquarters in Panama. The system was intended to collect information from mobile devices and could access communications and other data.

Pegasus was subsequently used by Panama's National Security Council to monitor more than 150 people, according to records cited in the U.S. extradition case against former president Ricardo Martinelli. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Israeli firm Candiru was founded in 2014 by Eran Shorer and Yaakov Weizman. It is thought to be Israel’s second-largest spyware maker after NSO Group. With funding from NSO investors as well as the government of Qatar, its systems have been found to have been operated by multiple countries, including Saudi Arabia, Israel, UAE, Hungary, Indonesia, and Uzbekistan. In November 2021, the US Commerce Department added Candiru and NSO to its trade blacklist.

According to Haaretz, the largest shareholder in Isaac Zack, who has been its chairman since the beginning and was also a founding funder of NSO. In 2021, malware manufactured by Candiru was found on the phones of politicians, journalists, and scholars in Iran, Yemen, Israel, the United Kingdom, and Turkey. Candiru has changed names multiple times, to Grindavik, then DF Associates, then Taveta, then Saito Tech, but it is still commonly known as Candiru. 

Researchers from Recorded Future's Insikt Group have identified active infrastructure associated with Candiru's spyware, known as DevilsTongue, in Hungary and Saudi Arabia. This spyware targets Windows systems and is believed to be deployed through spear-phishing emails, malicious links, and compromised websites.

In 2025, Integrity Partners, a U.S. investment firm, acquired Candiru’s assets for up to $30 million, moving its operations and staff to the new entity Integrity Labs Ltd., which is not subject to U.S. sanctions. The deal aims to bypass U.S. restrictions after Candiru was blacklisted in 2021 over national security concerns.

Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

children.text: Speech Technology Center (STC,) also known as SpeechPro, is a Russian company that develops speech recognition, facial recognition and voice biometrics. It has its origins linked to a secretive Soviet technologies unit that operated under the KGB. According to Wired, the company's roots can be traced back to the Sharashka Marfino, a special prison for engineers and scientists during the Stalin era. In this facility, individuals plucked from various labor camps were coerced into developing technologies, including voice identification systems used for monitoring calls to foreign embassies in Moscow. According to its website, it worked with Saudi's Ministry of Interior to install an audio forensic lab in the Kingdom.

In 2019, Sberbank, the state-controlled financial powerhouse, finalized the acquisition of a 51% stake in STC. Additionally, Digital Horizon, a venture capital and business incubator firm with offices in Moscow and Tel Aviv, also secured a stake in STC.

According to the BIRN (Balkan Investigative Reporting Network) investigation into surveillance systems in Serbia, STC's voice recognition software was procured by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MUP). Serbian intermediary companies, notably AIGO and IntellSec, facilitated the supply to Serbian state institutions.

children.text: IntellSec is a supplier of intelligence technology for government and industry contracts. Founded in 2017 by Milan Blagojevic, IntellSec distributes interceptions, geolocation, and digital forensics technologies, as well as bugsweeping tools. children.text: The Chinese government uses Hikvision's AI-enabled technology for mass surveillance and racial profiling. Beginning in 2016, authorities installed tens of thousands of Hikvision surveillance cameras in Ürümqi to monitor every movement of the Uyghur population in East Turkistan (renamed Xinjiang by China). The company was found to have received at least $275 million in government contracts to build surveillance in the region and has developed AI cameras that can detect physical features of Uyghur ethnicity. With over 600,000 Hikvision networks, the United States has the second-highest number of the company’s cameras, followed by Vietnam. In 2019, the US passed a bill banning Hikvision from holding any contracts with the federal government.

A Reuters report revealed that Myanmar's military junta installed Chinese-built facial recognition cameras in key urban centers to strengthen its surveillance capabilities, with technology provided by Hikvision alongside other Chinese surveillance giants, Zhejiang Dahua Technology and Huawei Technologies Co Ltd.
Hikvision is one of China's largest exporters of surveillance cameras and facial recognition tools.

children.text:
Naung Yoe Technologies Co., Ltd. is a Yangon-based company that distributes surveillance products, system integration, and equipment provision. Since the 2021 military coup, Naung Yoe Technologies has been involved in the procurement and installation of surveillance technologies across Myanmar. The company has been awarded tenders to install Chinese-made CCTV cameras equipped with facial recognition capabilities in several cities, including Naypyidaw. These projects are part of the junta's "safe city" initiatives. 

The surveillance systems supplied by Naung Yoe Technologies are sourced from Chinese manufacturers such as Zhejiang Dahua Technology, Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd., and Hikvision.

A source close to the company disclosed that Naung Yoe Technologies employed former generals, which may have influenced its success in securing government contracts, including the installation of CCTV networks and command-and-control centers in Naypyidaw. In March 2023, the company was added to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Entity List, which restricts access to U.S.-origin items, software, and technology.

Xinjiang Lianhai Chuangzhi Information Technology Co., Ltd. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC), a large state-owned military contractor. The company supplies the Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP) system, which is a major component in the region’s surveillance infrastructure. The IJOP is described in multiple reports as a "system of systems" that aggregates data from many sources: facial recognition cameras, CCTV, checkpoints, and a wide range of apps. 

The company has built AI-powered checkpoint systems that can detect and track individuals, particularly Uyghurs, as they move around cities. These systems integrate facial recognition, cameras, and other biometric monitoring.

The U.S. Department of Commerce added the company to its Entity List on July 9, 2021, along with 13 other Chinese companies which were sanctioned for their involvement in human rights abuses and surveillance activities in Xinjiang.

children.text: Avigilon, a subsidiary of Motorola Solutions, designs, develops, and manufactures high-definition cameras, video management software, and AI-powered analytics tools. One of the company's developments is the Avigilon Appearance Search technology, an AI-powered tool embedded in their Avigilon Control Center (ACC) video management software. This technology allows customers to search for individuals based on specific physical characteristics, such as hair and clothing color, gender, and age. Avigilon's cameras are used in prisons, airports, schools and government facilities.

In 2024, San Diego State University installed over 1,300 Avigilon AI cameras for more than $1.3 million, with over 330 in student dorms. The company states the cameras can perform facial recognition, license plate recognition, and behavior analysis. Students were not informed of the installation, learning its scope only through a Daily Aztec investigation.

In 2015, Axis was acquired by Canon Inc.

Honorlock is a remote proctoring service used widely by U.S. colleges and universities to monitor students during online exams. The platform installs as a Chrome extension that activates during exams to lock down the browser, while its AI watches for "suspicious behavior" and pings a live proctor to intervene via chat as soon as something is flagged.

During a session, Honorlock captures webcam video of the test-taker, microphone audio of the room, the full screen, and keystroke and tab-switching activity; it also requires a 360-degree room scan and government-issued ID verification before the exam begins. Beyond the local machine, the company runs "search-and-destroy" honeypot sites (decoy pages seeded with leaked test questions) to detect when students try to look up answers on a second device, an approach students have characterized as entrapment.

children.text:
Landasoft is a Shanghai-based private defense company and technology firm that contributes to China's mass surveillance infrastructure, particularly in the Xinjiang province. An Associated Press investigation revealed that the firm, which was a former partner of IBM, replicated IBM's i2 police analytics and launched its own platform to power the Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP) in Xinjiang. 

Landasoft deployed software that scraped data from millions of cameras, police outposts, and personal records to build risk dossiers. The system categorized individuals using tags like "studied abroad" or "went on pilgrimage," computed risk scores, and enabled automatic “Push Alerts” to trigger detentions based on flawed predictions, often without human oversight. In one week in 2017 alone, IJOP flagged 24,412 people as "suspicious," leading to widespread detentions, with Uyghurs as a primary target.

children.text: Sandvine was founded in 2001 in Waterloo, Ontario, by a team of ~30 people from PixStream (a Cisco acquisition).

The company developed deep packet inspection (DPI) technology for network traffic management, which is also used for censorship and surveillance purposes. In 2017, San Francisco-based private equity firm Francisco Partners acquired Sandvine and merged it with its U.S.-based holding Procera Networks in a deal valued at approximately $562 million. Procera had separately developed DPI technology that was used for surveillance and censorship in countries with authoritarian regimes.

Following the merger, Sandvine struck deals with several governments, including in Belarus, Egypt, Eritrea, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. By 2023, Egypt alone accounted for $26 million in annual sales, roughly 13% of the company's total revenue. That same year, researchers at Citizen Lab discovered Sandvine's technology had been used in attempts to inject spyware into the iPhone of Ahmed Eltantawy, an Egyptian politician planning to challenge President El-Sisi.

In February 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department added Sandvine to its Entity List for providing Egypt with "mass web-monitoring and censorship" technology used to block news and target political actors and human rights activists. The blacklisting effectively banned Sandvine from obtaining U.S. technology, and major firms including Microsoft, Zoom, and Intel cut ties with the company. Francisco Partners exited its ownership in August 2024
The DOC removed Sandvine from the Entity List in October, 2024, after the company promised to "undergo transformative changes."
The company has since rebranded to AppLogic Networks.

children.text:
Landasoft is a Shanghai-based private defense company and technology firm that contributes to China's mass surveillance infrastructure, particularly in the Xinjiang province. An Associated Press investigation revealed that the firm, which was a former partner of IBM, replicated IBM's i2 police analytics and launched its own platform to power the Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP) in Xinjiang. 

Landasoft deployed software that scraped data from millions of cameras, police outposts, and personal records to build risk dossiers. The system categorized individuals using tags like "studied abroad" or "went on pilgrimage," computed risk scores, and enabled automatic “Push Alerts” to trigger detentions based on flawed predictions, often without human oversight. In one week in 2017 alone, IJOP flagged 24,412 people as "suspicious," leading to widespread detentions, with Uyghurs as a primary target.

children.text: IBM used New York's CCTV cameras footage without public knowledge to develop surveillance software. The software can search for individuals based on age, gender, and skin tone. children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: Inpixon is a location intelligence company that develops real-time location systems (RTLS) capable of tracking people and devices.

Its technology uses Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, UWB, and other radio frequency signals to identify and locate devices and can provide continuous location data, movement histories, geofencing, and real-time tracking. Inpixon's technology has also been deployed for student monitoring. A report in 2020 found that the company was in "various stages of negotiations" for U.S. schools to install Inpixon radio frequency scanners capable of detecting Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals from students' phones and locating them. According to CNET, marketing material from the company showed that its wristbands aimed for younger children also tracks their biometrics.
The company's CEO said it was also in discussions with additional school districts and that schools in the Middle East were considering the technology.
The company provides its technology for prisons, malls, and locations, without awareness from people that their data is being collected.
Inpixon merged with XTI Aircraft Company in March 2024, creating XTI Aerospace. In February 2026, the Inpixon business was acquired by an investor group and became privately held.
