Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Formerly known as Equus Technologies, Merlinx is an Israeli spyware firm specializing in cyber infiltration tools, founded by former Israeli army technical intelligence specialists Matan Markovics, Daniel Hanga, and Tal Tchwella. In 2021, the company was acquired by Israeli-US cloud data company OwnBackup. Merlinx has gained attention for its collaboration with Bangladesh's National Security Intelligence (NSI), facilitated through a contract with Israeli-Cyprus integrator Prelysis, led by Amit Aisikowitz.

Merlinx provides advanced surveillance tools, including its Apollo platform, which enables Wifi interception and phishing-based data extraction. The system can intercept unsecured URL communications, extract email identifiers, and deploy cyber agents capable of infiltrating Android devices to access data, activate GPS tracking, and log keystrokes. This technology is part of Bangladesh's tactical cyber intelligence operations, known to be used against journalists, dissidents and human rights defenders.

Merlinx is now owned by Bindecy. Bindecy, co-founded by Eylon Ben Yaakov and Daniel Shapiro, has ties to the Israeli cyber-intelligence firm Toka, as both founders previously worked at KayHut, a company led by Toka's co-founder Kfir Waldman.

According to Google researchers, Lipizzan is a multi-stage spyware capable of monitoring and extracting a user’s emails, SMS messages, location data, voice calls, and media files. Google identified 20 Lipizzan apps, which were distributed in a highly targeted manner to fewer than 100 devices. In response, Google has blocked both the developers and the apps from the Android ecosystem. Besides malware, the source reported that Equus Technologies also offers app and cloud interception technology packaged as portable devices. At least one employee of Equus Technologies is a former staff member of NSO Group, the notorious Israeli malware vendor.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Operation Zero is a Russian zero-day exploit brokerage operating under the legal entity Matrix LLC, owned by Sergey Sergeyevich Zelenyuk. The company has openly stated it will only sell exploits to customers in non-NATO countries, including the Russian government and foreign intelligence agencies. Beyond exploit brokering, Operation Zero has also pursued the development of spyware and tools to extract personal data from users of AI applications such as large language models.

Operation Zero came further into the spotlight when it was revealed that Peter Williams, a 39-year-old Australian national and former executive at U.S. defense contractor L3Harris, stole eight classified zero-day exploits from his employer between 2022 and 2025 and sold them to Operation Zero for millions of dollars. Operation Zero then re-sold these stolen tools, originally intended solely for the U.S. government and its allies, to unauthorized users. Williams was sentenced to over seven years in federal prison after pleading guilty.

In February 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Zelenyuk, Operation Zero / Matrix LLC, and several associates, including Azizjon Makhmudovich Mamashoyev and Oleg Vyacheslavovich Kucherov (a suspected member of the Trickbot cybercrime gang), for their role in acquiring and distributing cyber tools.

Zelenyuk also established a UAE-based technology company called STS specifically to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Russian bank accounts and to conduct business with entities in Asia and the Middle East. STS was among the entities sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury in February 2026 alongside Zelenyuk and Operation Zero.

children.text: Coruna is an iPhone hacking toolkit first identified by security researchers in February 2025. According to mobile security company iVerify and reporting by TechCrunch, the exploit kit is believed to have been created by the hacking and surveillance division of US military contractor L3Harris and developed for use by the US government.

According to Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which named the toolkit, Coruna contains five complete iOS exploit chains leveraging a total of 23 distinct vulnerabilities, targeting iPhones running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1. The kit primarily exploits Apple's WebKit browser framework, enabling "watering hole" attacks that silently compromise a device when a user simply visits a malicious website. The toolkit is estimated to have infected tens of thousands of phones worldwide.

Coruna has also proliferated beyond its original operator. Google tracked its use by a suspected Russian espionage group (UNC6353) in watering hole attacks targeting Ukrainian users, and later by a financially motivated Chinese cybercriminal operation (UNC6691) stealing cryptocurrency. The exact mechanism of proliferation remains unclear, but Google says it points to an active market for "second-hand" zero-day exploits and unscrupulous brokers facilitating the spread of nation-state-grade tools to criminals and foreign intelligence services.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. children.text: Oracle develops and helps resource AI-powered surveillance technologies. Through its Oracle Public Safety Services Suite, the company provides tools such as body cameras, real-time monitoring systems, and cloud-based dispatch centers for law enforcement. These systems are designed to enable continuous, real-time monitoring, with features like body cameras that cannot be turned off by officers to ensure constant data collection.

Larry Ellison, Oracle's co-founder, has openly advocated for a vision of mass AI surveillance. This vision includes leveraging Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) and advanced AI to track activities and behaviors in real time. Oracle's CEO and longtime executive, Safra A. Catz, is on the Board of Trustees of In-Q-Tel, a venture capital firm funded by the CIA, and which invests in social media monitoring and surveillance tools to support U.S. intelligence operations.

Oracle's Endeca Information Discovery software was used by the Chicago Police Department during the 2012 NATO protests to monitor and analyze social media activity, including tweets from protesters, in real time. The software, backed by CIA funding, enabled police to merge social media data with crime records and 911 calls, allowing targeted surveillance of individuals and sentiment analysis of posts. Oracle later marketed this technology globally, including to Chinese authorities.

In 2024, Oracle agreed to a $115 million settlement to resolve a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of unlawfully collecting and selling personal data without user consent. The lawsuit alleged that Oracle tracked individuals' online and offline activities, compiled detailed profiles, and sold this data through its advertising platforms, such as the ID Graph and Data Marketplace.

children.text:
Mühlbauer, a German technology company, became Uganda's first biometric ID system provider in 2010 following a meeting between President Museveni and the German ambassador. The $80 million contract was controversial as it bypassed normal government procurement rules by avoiding a competitive bidding process. The company played a significant role in expanding Uganda's biometric identity coverage, registering approximately 5 million citizens in just 6 weeks. While Mühlbauer's technology was ostensibly implemented for legitimate identification purposes, extensive documentation and interviews gathered by Bloomberg and nonprofit investigative newsroom Lighthouse Reports reveal it has evolved into a sophisticated surveillance tool used to monitor politicians, journalists, human rights advocates, and ordinary citizens in Uganda.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: RCS Lab is an Italian company specializing in the development and sale of surveillance and interception technologies. Founded in 1993 and headquartered in Milan, RCS Lab provides a range of services and products to law enforcement and intelligence agencies worldwide. In 2022, Cy4Gate acquired fellow Italian firm RCS Lab, known for its “Hermit” spyware tools. Google and Meta have observed RCS Lab campaigns in Italy, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Mongolia. Tykelab, a company based in Rome and owned by RCS Lab, had been using dozens of phone networks, often on islands in the South Pacific, to send tens of thousands of secret ‘tracking packets’ around the world, targeting people in countries including Italy itself, Greece, North Macedonia, Portugal, Libya, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Malaysia, Iraq and Mali. RCS Lab has offshoots in France, Germany and Spain, as well as another concealed subsidiary, Azienda Informatica Italiana, which builds interception software for Android and iPhone devices.

children.text: Hacking Team was a Milan-based Italian company that sold spyware capabilities to governments, law enforcement agencies, and corporations worldwide. Hacking Team's Remote Control System (RCS) could be deployed using exploits to a target's computer or cell phone, with the ability to track an individual's movements, log their keystrokes, and even activate their computer camera.

In July 2015, hackers infiltrated Hacking Team's network and leaked over 400 GB of sensitive internal data, including emails, financial documents, zero-day exploits, the source code for RCS, and a spreadsheet listing its government clients. The hackers also took over the company's Twitter account, using it to post screenshots of emails and other internal details.
Despite the severity of the breach, Hacking Team resumed operations and began working with a new set of tools.

Though widely thought to be defunct after the 2015 exposure, the company effectively re-emerged under Memento Labs. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber, continuing to develop surveillance software.
In 2025, researchers linked Memento Labs to a new spyware called Dante, confirming that the entity once known as Hacking Team remained active in the commercial spyware market.

children.text:
Memento Labs is a company that acquired the infamous spyware vendor Hacking Team, which sold its surveillance technology, called Remote Control System (RCS), to governments and dictatorships worldwide. When researchers began to uncover information about Hacking Team’s operations, the primary targets were human rights activists and journalists. Hacking Team's former chairman, Paolo Lezzi, became the owner of Memento Labs and its parent company, InTheCyber. Memento Labs develops various snooping products, such as KRAIT, a surveillance tool that can silently infect any Android device without the target’s knowledge. It uses a "trusted implant" to appear as a legitimate source, making it easy to trick users into installing it. Once installed, KRAIT can steal passwords, monitor the device's location, microphone, camera, calls, and messages, all while hiding its activity through trusted online services. Another product, RCS X, is the latest version of a powerful spyware that has been used against journalists and human rights activists since 2012. It can infect almost any device, including macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and BlackBerry, using security vulnerabilities. Once installed, RCS X allows hackers to control microphones, cameras, and take screenshots, while managing all infections from a single console. 

At a monitoring conference in Dubai, Memento Labs introduced two new tools: MoniTOR and PrevenTer. PrevenTer is designed for speech recognition and transcribing call recordings. MoniTOR is aimed at helping law enforcement track activities by attempting to exploit any technical vulnerabilities to bypass anonymization methods used by the Tor network. However, these tools were not developed by the company itself, it was developed via a research collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI) and funded by the Swiss Agency for Innovation Promotion, Innosuisse. SUPSI and Memento Labs' parent company, In The Cyber, have contractual agreements to jointly develop software products.
In 2025, Memento Labs' CEO confirmed that one of its government clients was caught using its Dante spyware.

children.text: RCS Lab is an Italian company specializing in the development and sale of surveillance and interception technologies. Founded in 1993 and headquartered in Milan, RCS Lab provides a range of services and products to law enforcement and intelligence agencies worldwide. In 2022, Cy4Gate acquired fellow Italian firm RCS Lab, known for its “Hermit” spyware tools. Google and Meta have observed RCS Lab campaigns in Italy, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Mongolia. Tykelab, a company based in Rome and owned by RCS Lab, had been using dozens of phone networks, often on islands in the South Pacific, to send tens of thousands of secret ‘tracking packets’ around the world, targeting people in countries including Italy itself, Greece, North Macedonia, Portugal, Libya, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Malaysia, Iraq and Mali. RCS Lab has offshoots in France, Germany and Spain, as well as another concealed subsidiary, Azienda Informatica Italiana, which builds interception software for Android and iPhone devices.

This system, which includes tools from other Israeli companies, has been criticized for creating "prison-like" conditions for refugees. The refugee camps, such as the one on the island of Samos, have been described as "testing grounds" for surveillance technologies later deployed elsewhere in Europe.

Viisights' behavioral video analytics are also used by Israel's Ministry of Public Security and in smart city initiatives, such as in the city of Eilat, to detect and analyze events in real-time.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.

children.text: Mobile Companion is a field-ready app used by the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers that functions as a real-time vehicle surveillance tool. Powered by Motorola Solutions and Thomson Reuters, the app allows officers to instantly scan a license plate and cross-reference it against a database containing billions of records, revealing where that vehicle has been spotted across the U.S. The app can also predict where a car may travel in the future.

Beyond vehicle tracking, Mobile Companion aggregates a wide range of personal data, including driver license records, credit header data, marriage records, vehicle ownership, and voter registrations, allowing officers to quickly build a profile on a vehicle's owner. The app can also collect face scans for facial recognition purposes. It is designed to operate similarly to ICE's existing facial recognition apps but is specifically focused on gathering intelligence about vehicles and their owners.

children.text: Equifax is one of the three major U.S. consumer credit reporting bureaus. Operating as a data broker, its products provide U.S. immigration authorities and law enforcement with information used to locate people targeted for arrest and deportation. Between 2005 and September 2024, the U.S Department of Homeland Security (DHS) awarded Equifax contracts worth at least $16.1 million, while total U.S. federal government contracts with the company exceeded $365 million during the same period.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

name: Mobile Identify

children.text: Mobile Identify is a facial recognition application developed by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and distributed through Google's Play Store to local law enforcement agencies that have been deputized to work with federal immigration authorities. The app enables officers to scan faces and identify individuals by searching federal databases, functioning similarly to the Mobile Fortify app used directly by ICE agents.

The app is specifically designed to support local law enforcement officers working under the 287(g) program, a federal partnership that allows state and local police to perform immigration enforcement functions.

By making this technology available through a public app store, CBP effectively extended federal facial recognition capabilities to a broader network of local agencies participating in immigration enforcement operations. However, in December 2025, the app was removed from the Google Play Store amid scrutiny over its use by law enforcement without public oversight or clear legal authority.

name: Mobile Innovations

children.text: Mobile Innovations is a Spanish company based in Madrid and the parent behind the OwnSpy consumer stalkerware product. Beyond OwnSpy, the company has operated a family of related mobile tracking and spoofing apps, including iLocalis, iGotYa, and FakeLocation.

The company's most well known app, OwnSpy, is stalkerware that is covertly installed on a target's device and streams its contents (messages, calls, photos, and location) to a dashboard viewable by whoever planted it. Unlike most phone monitoring apps, OwnSpy does not simply hide from the home screen but disguises itself as an Android system Wi-Fi app.

Investigative reporting found that the Brazil based WebDetetive was effectively a repackaged copy of OwnSpy's spyware, built on a commission model in which third parties promote the app and OwnSpy takes a cut. Independent research has concluded that reseller sites such as WebDetetive and SaferSpy are most likely operated in large part by Mobile Innovations itself, citing shared infrastructure and near simultaneous vulnerability fixes across those sites.

In July 2022, WhatsApp sued Mobile Innovations and its founder Antonio José Calatrava Pérez in a Madrid commercial court, alleging that OwnSpy and a related app, Wossip, infringed WhatsApp's IP rights, constituted unfair competition, and violated its terms of use by capturing users' messages, calls, status, online activity, and profile data. The parties settled: Mobile Innovations agreed to cease and desist from developing or operating Wossip and to delete all copies, to strip OwnSpy of all functionality targeting WhatsApp and other Meta platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Oculus), to stop using the associated trademarks, and to pay a monetary penalty.

In 2023, WebDetetive suffered a major data breach that exposed internal company data and customer information, including credentials and data linked to monitored devices. Mobilewalla is a data broker and consumer intelligence platform that aggregates and analyzes large amounts of consumer data. It was founded in Singapore and later moved its headquarters to Atlanta, Georgia, U.S.

Mobilewalla collected over 500 million unique consumer advertising identifiers paired with precise location data, often without consumer knowledge or consent. This data revealed sensitive information, such as visits to healthcare facilities, religious institutions, and political events. Mobilewalla also tracked residents of domestic abuse shelters and purposefully tracked protesters in 2020.

In addition, Mobilewalla admitted that it supplied data used by the U.S Department of Homeland Security, the U.S Internal Revenue Service (IRS), and the U.S. military for warrantless device tracking domestically and internationally.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) stated that Mobilewalla failed to anonymize this data. In response to these practices, the FTC finalized an order in 2025 banning Mobilewalla from selling sensitive location data and collecting consumer data.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: Mollitiam Industries is a Spanish cybersecurity and surveillance company that develops intelligence and monitoring solutions. The company provides various tools with intelligence gathering and surveillance capabilities for both government and private sector clients. Those who have bought its surveillance products include the Colombian armed forces, which have used them to illegally spy on supreme court judges, politicians, journalists, and journalists’ sources. Colombian targets have included Alejandro Santos, the editor of the news magazine Semana, and some of his reporters after they published articles about crimes committed by the members of the military. In 2019 alone, Colombia’s military reportedly spent $800,000 on spyware from Mollitiam Industries.
According to TechCrunch, as of early 2025, the company has shut down.

children.text: MSAB is a Swedish forensic technology company. Its software, XRY, which can decrypt passwords and recover deleted data, was reportedly used by Hong Kong police in 2020 to access pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong's phone in under an hour.  Leaked documents in 2021 showed that Myanmar's military junta used MSAB's technology to extract data from phones, including deleted content. In the U.S, the San Diego Police Department employs MSAB's XRY software to extract data from mobile devices in investigations. It's also used by the FBI and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB), among other government agencies.

MSAB developed tools for CPB to gather information from vehicles at border crossings by extracting data from car infotainment systems. These systems store a wealth of information, including call logs, text messages, GPS locations, and paired device data.
MSAB's phone extraction tools were also supplied to Moroccan authorities under EU-funded border management programs to surveil migrants transiting North Africa.
Its reseller in Hong Kong is S-Tech, which also sells surveillance tools from Oxygen Forensics and BlackBag (acquired by Cellebrite in 2020.)

children.text:
BadBazaar is a mobile spyware tool with variants targeting both Android and iOS devices. It has been linked to Chinese-backed hacking groups, such as APT15. This group is known by various names assigned by different cybersecurity organizations, including Vixen Panda, Ke3chang, Nickel, Playful Taurus, BackdoorDiplomacy, Mirage, GREF, RoyalAPT, Nylon Typhoon, Flea, and Red Vulture. 

BadBazaar has primarily been used to target Uyghur, Tibetan, and Taiwanese individuals, as well as civil society actors who may oppose Chinese state interests.

The spyware is distributed through trojanized apps, including fake versions of popular communication tools like Signal and Telegram, as well as apps tailored to specific communities, such as Uyghur-language Quran apps. Once installed, BadBazaar can collect sensitive data, including call logs, GPS locations, SMS messages, and files. The spyware has also been observed spreading via social media platforms and official app stores.

The Chengdu-based contractor, Sichuan Dianke Network Security Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as UPSEC), was linked to the deployment of this malware.

children.text: DarkNimbus is a cross platform spyware and remote access trojan (RAT) linked to the threat actor Earth Minotaur. First documented in 2025, it has been deployed against Uyghur and Tibetan communities after being delivered through the Moonshine exploit framework, which abuses vulnerabilities in WeChat and Chromium based applications.

Once installed, DarkNimbus enables extensive surveillance by collecting contacts, SMS messages, call logs, browser data, and messaging app conversations, while also tracking device location, recording phone calls, capturing screenshots and photos, transferring files, and executing remote commands.

Security researchers have linked the broader activity of Earth Minotaur and related Chinese state-aligned operators to targeting ethnic minority groups, human rights advocates, and individuals considered politically sensitive by Beijing.

children.text: WeChat, known as Weixin in China, is a multifunctional messaging app developed by Tencent. It has become one of the most popular social networking platforms in China and is widely used for communication, social networking, mobile payments, and more. Users are required to register with their real identities, tying their activities on WeChat to their personal information. This facilitates tracking and monitoring by authorities. Tencent, the company behind WeChat, complies with Chinese government requests for user data and content removal. This includes providing access to user communications and metadata under legal requirements. An investigation by Citizen Lab revealed that WeChat conducts surveillance of images and files shared on the platform, even for users outside of China. This surveillance is used to train censorship algorithms and build up the censorship system for WeChat's China-registered users. WeChat scans documents for sensitive text and images for both text and visual content, flagging MD5 hashes (a kind of digital fingerprint) of politically sensitive files. In 2020, it was revealed that WeChat conducts extensive content surveillance on communications among non-China-registered accounts as well.

Bogle, Vanguard is headquartered in Malvern, Pennsylvania, and manages trillions of dollars in assets globally.

BlackRock Inc. is the world's largest asset management firm, headquartered in New York City. Known for managing a diverse range of investment products and services, BlackRock oversees trillions of dollars in assets across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and cash management strategies.

State Street was founded in 1792, making it one of the oldest financial institutions in the United States. State Street operates globally, with offices in major financial centers around the world. Its headquarters are located in Boston, Massachusetts, USA.

Capital World Investors is one of the equity investment divisions of Capital Group (operating under Capital Research and Management Company), among the world's oldest and largest investment management organizations, founded in Los Angeles in 1931.

Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is the asset management division of Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, responsible for the operational management of the Government Pension Fund Global (the Norwegian "oil fund") on behalf of the Ministry of Finance, making it the world's largest sovereign wealth fund with over US$2 trillion in assets. NBIM is headquartered in Oslo, Norway, with additional offices in London, New York, and Singapore.

UBS Asset Management is the asset management division of UBS Group AG, the largest Swiss banking institution and one of the world's leading financial services firms, overseeing roughly US$2 trillion in assets. UBS Asset Management operates as part of UBS Group AG, which is headquartered in Zurich and Basel, Switzerland.

Motorola Solutions, Inc. is a Chicago-based communications company that sells radio systems, body cameras, facial recognition technology, license plate readers, and AI-driven surveillance software primarily to government agencies. The company is a documented contractor and vendor for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), supplying equipment, communications systems, and surveillance products used to expand immigration enforcement capacity.

Motorola's 2019 acquisition of VaaS International Holdings, parent company of Vigilant Solutions, gave the company control of one of the largest automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks in the United States. ICE holds a $22.8 million contract for access to Vigilant's ALPR database.

Motorola Solutions has maintained an extensive relationship with Israeli security forces through its subsidiary, Motorola Solutions Israel. The company's surveillance equipment has been installed in illegal Israeli settlements, along the separation wall in the occupied West Bank, in Gaza, and at Israeli military bases. Israel's Ministry of Defense awarded Motorola a contract for the MotoEagle Wide Area Surveillance System (WASS), a radar-based "virtual fence" deployed to dozens of illegal settlements in a NIS 400 million project.
Motorola Solutions has been included on the United Nations database of companies involved in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. Their offerings include video management systems, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) software, and real-time crime center (RTCC) analytics to expand police surveillance networks. Genetec also leads a program to facilitate the process for law enforcement agencies to request and retrieve footage from private cameras.

In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Powered by Microsoft Azure, Citigraf integrates information from surveillance sensors and database records, using both real-time and historical data to generate calculations, visualizations, and alerts that provide CPD with "deep situational awareness." Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.
Microsoft has long provided facial recognition services to law enforcement through its extensive partnerships with Genetic and similar companies.

children.text: Mal-Tech Technological Solutions Ltd. is an Israeli security technology company that provides surveillance and related systems for police, military, law enforcement, and "safe city" projects, including CCTV networks, video management systems, video analytics, and sensors.

Amnesty International identified Mal-Tech as the Israeli distributor for Dutch surveillance company TKH Security in 2017 and raised concerns that TKH cameras installed in occupied East Jerusalem could be used with Israel's Mabat 2000 facial recognition system to surveil and track Palestinians.

children.text: Founded in 2009 by Chris Bennet, Callyo is a Florida-based provider of surveillance tools for U.S. federal and law enforcement agencies. The company's tools enable tracking of locations, interception of calls, and turning smartphones into covert recording devices - all without the user's knowledge. One of Callyo's unique features is its ability to facilitate international wiretapping without requiring authorization from local authorities. By intercepting calls and routing them through virtual numbers to its servers, the software ensures that investigators can listen to and record conversations undetected. In Massachusetts, the Boston Police Department and State Police have faced scrutiny for using Callyo's app without obtaining proper warrants. An internal audit revealed that Massachusetts State Police had used the app in at least 250 cases without proper disclosure.
The company was acquired by Motorola Solutions in 2020.

children.text: Avigilon, a subsidiary of Motorola Solutions, designs, develops, and manufactures high-definition cameras, video management software, and AI-powered analytics tools. One of the company's developments is the Avigilon Appearance Search technology, an AI-powered tool embedded in their Avigilon Control Center (ACC) video management software. This technology allows customers to search for individuals based on specific physical characteristics, such as hair and clothing color, gender, and age. Avigilon's cameras are used in prisons, airports, schools and government facilities.

In 2024, San Diego State University installed over 1,300 Avigilon AI cameras for more than $1.3 million, with over 330 in student dorms. The company states the cameras can perform facial recognition, license plate recognition, and behavior analysis. Students were not informed of the installation, learning its scope only through a Daily Aztec investigation.

entity.name: Mal-Tech

children.text: Mal-Tech Technological Solutions Ltd. is an Israeli security technology company that provides surveillance and related systems for police, military, law enforcement, and "safe city" projects, including CCTV networks, video management systems, video analytics, and sensors.

The company says it deployed more than 3,000 CCTV cameras and multiple control rooms as part of Jerusalem’s "Smart & Safe City" project between 2015 and 2023. Amnesty International identified Mal-Tech as the Israeli distributor for Dutch surveillance company TKH Security in 2017 and raised concerns that TKH cameras installed in occupied East Jerusalem could be used with Israel's Mabat 2000 facial recognition system to surveil and track Palestinians.

Amnesty noted that TKH cameras were found in public spaces and attached to police infrastructure, while TKH told Amnesty it had not done business with Mal-Tech in recent years and had no current direct relationship with Israeli security forces. Mal-Tech is also the official Israeli distributor for Italian video surveillance manufacturer VideoTec (now owned by Motorola Solutions), whose cameras have been documented in East Jerusalem.

children.text: Genetec is a prominent provider of surveillance technology, supplying law enforcement with a range of invasive monitoring tools. In 2017, Genetec developed the Citigraf platform specifically for the Chicago Police Department (CPD), one of the largest police forces in the U.S., to help manage and analyze their extensive data collection. Microsoft is collaborating with Genetec to advance this platform with a "correlation engine" designed to interpret surveillance data more effectively. In 2016, the city of Detroit in Michigan launched Project Green Light, which uses Genetec Stratocast and Microsoft Azure to stream surveillance footage from local businesses and other entities to the Detroit Police Department.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: MSAB is a Swedish forensic technology company. Its software, XRY, which can decrypt passwords and recover deleted data, was reportedly used by Hong Kong police in 2020 to access pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong's phone in under an hour.  Leaked documents in 2021 showed that Myanmar's military junta used MSAB's technology to extract data from phones, including deleted content. In the U.S, the San Diego Police Department employs MSAB's XRY software to extract data from mobile devices in investigations. It's also used by the FBI and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB), among other government agencies.

MSAB developed tools for CPB to gather information from vehicles at border crossings by extracting data from car infotainment systems. These systems store a wealth of information, including call logs, text messages, GPS locations, and paired device data.
MSAB's phone extraction tools were also supplied to Moroccan authorities under EU-funded border management programs to surveil migrants transiting North Africa.
Its reseller in Hong Kong is S-Tech, which also sells surveillance tools from Oxygen Forensics and BlackBag (acquired by Cellebrite in 2020.)

The company claims its technology can access data from over 6,700 car models globally.
Among the agencies that rely on iVe is U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Berla has collaborated with MSAB since 2016 to integrate Berla iVe's hardware with MSAB's XAMN analytics software.

children.text: Oxygen Software, a Russia-based company, develops mobile forensics tools marketed under its U.S branch, Oxygen Forensics. These tools are primarily deployed by government agencies and are widely used for surveillance purposes. Their capabilities include extracting vast amounts of data from mobile devices, such as personal messages, call logs, location data, and other sensitive information. Governments, particularly in Central Asia, such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, have reportedly used them to monitor activists, journalists, and political dissidents. In the U.S, its tools are used by the U.S Army, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), alongside other government agencies. According to an investigation by Gizmodo, U.S. school districts are also amongst its users. For example, Cypress-Fairbanks ISD in Texas confirmed using Oxygen Forensics' tools to extract data from students' phones for "evidentiary purposes."

Oxygen Forensics' tools have also been supplied to Morocco as part of an EU funded program. According to an investigation by Disclose, Oxygen Forensics provided the Moroccan police with a data extraction and analysis system called "Detective," which can bypass locked phone screens to retrieve information stored on cloud computing platforms managed by Google, Microsoft, and Apple, as well as hack supposedly secure applications on any mobile phone or computer.
Oxygen Software’s tools are often sold through regional resellers, such as Softline, which has offices in Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

In September 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the arrests of Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Davydov on allegations that they concealed the company’s Russian ownership and the fact that its software was developed in Russia while obtaining contracts from U.S. government agencies.

Its GrayKey product is a forensic access tool that enables the extraction of encrypted or inaccessible data from mobile devices, including those protected by alphanumeric passcodes.

In 2023, Grayshift merged with Magnet Forensics, a Canadian digital forensics company, to create a combined entity focused on providing advanced digital investigation tools to law enforcement and public safety agencies.

children.text: MSAB is a Swedish forensic technology company. Its software, XRY, which can decrypt passwords and recover deleted data, was reportedly used by Hong Kong police in 2020 to access pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong's phone in under an hour.  Leaked documents in 2021 showed that Myanmar's military junta used MSAB's technology to extract data from phones, including deleted content. In the U.S, the San Diego Police Department employs MSAB's XRY software to extract data from mobile devices in investigations. It's also used by the FBI and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB), among other government agencies.

MSAB developed tools for CPB to gather information from vehicles at border crossings by extracting data from car infotainment systems. These systems store a wealth of information, including call logs, text messages, GPS locations, and paired device data.
MSAB's phone extraction tools were also supplied to Moroccan authorities under EU-funded border management programs to surveil migrants transiting North Africa.
Its reseller in Hong Kong is S-Tech, which also sells surveillance tools from Oxygen Forensics and BlackBag (acquired by Cellebrite in 2020.)

children.text: MVM Inc. is a private security contractor headquartered in Ashburn, Virginia. Under a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) contract, MVM operatives are tasked with surveilling and physically tracking down undocumented migrant children who came to the U.S. unaccompanied, visiting their homes and schools under the banner of "safety and wellness checks." Internal documents cited by the Guardian suggest those visits are less about child welfare than about gathering information to deport the kids or build cases against their sponsors.

children.text: Capital Systems LLC is a Georgian technology company that served as the local implementation partner for NEC Corporation’s facial recognition surveillance deployment in Georgia. children.text: Cognitec Systems is a face recognition technology company. One of its products, FaceVACS, delivers extensive surveillance functionality that goes beyond basic face matching. The system can guess ethnicity based on a person's skin color, flag suspects on watch lists, estimate the age of a person, detect gender, and "track" faces in real time. children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: Speech Technology Center (STC,) also known as SpeechPro, is a Russian company that develops speech recognition, facial recognition and voice biometrics. It has its origins linked to a secretive Soviet technologies unit that operated under the KGB. According to Wired, the company's roots can be traced back to the Sharashka Marfino, a special prison for engineers and scientists during the Stalin era. In this facility, individuals plucked from various labor camps were coerced into developing technologies, including voice identification systems used for monitoring calls to foreign embassies in Moscow. According to its website, it worked with Saudi's Ministry of Interior to install an audio forensic lab in the Kingdom.

In 2019, Sberbank, the state-controlled financial powerhouse, finalized the acquisition of a 51% stake in STC. Additionally, Digital Horizon, a venture capital and business incubator firm with offices in Moscow and Tel Aviv, also secured a stake in STC.

According to the BIRN (Balkan Investigative Reporting Network) investigation into surveillance systems in Serbia, STC's voice recognition software was procured by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MUP). Serbian intermediary companies, notably AIGO and IntellSec, facilitated the supply to Serbian state institutions.

children.text: Negg Group, an Italian cybersecurity firm, was first revealed in 2017 by Kaspersky as the developer of the “VBiss” and “Skygofree” Android malware, which can infect mobile devices through one-click exploit chains or by drive-by downloads. Google discovered targets in Italy, Malaysia, and Kazakhstan.

Negg's spyware tools can reportedly record audio and capture phone activity, including activating recording when a device enters a sensitive location, force infected devices onto attacker-controlled Wi-Fi networks for data collection, and exploit vulnerabilities to read encrypted WhatsApp messages.

In 2024, Meta took down a network of fake Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to Negg and seven other firms as part of a crackdown on commercial spyware operators.

Negg established a presence in the United Arab Emirates by joining a consortium for the Aion Sentia project in Abu Dhabi, which aims to develop an AI-powered city.

children.text:
NeoBit, a Russian company headquartered in St. Petersburg, is involved in surveillance and cyber operations on behalf of the Russian government. The company is behind the development of Vepr, a system designed to monitor and predict "information tension points" on the internet. This project, commissioned by Roskomnadzor (Russia's internet censorship agency), aims to analyze online content, including tone, aggression, and repost metrics, to identify perceived threats such as criticism of authorities, "LGBT propaganda," and other topics deemed undesirable by the state. Vepr is part of a broader initiative, the Clean Internet project, which seeks to surveil 100% of Russia's online activity using advanced neural networks and bot farms capable of infiltrating closed social media groups.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

Naung Yoe Technologies Co., Ltd. is a Yangon-based company that distributes surveillance products, system integration, and equipment provision. Since the 2021 military coup, Naung Yoe Technologies has been involved in the procurement and installation of surveillance technologies across Myanmar. The company has been awarded tenders to install Chinese-made CCTV cameras equipped with facial recognition capabilities in several cities, including Naypyidaw. The surveillance systems supplied by Naung Yoe Technologies are sourced from Chinese manufacturers such as Zhejiang Dahua Technology, Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd., and Hikvision.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text:
Almenta is a surveillance firm based in Bulgaria and run by Israeli operators, including CEO Ari Covitz. It develops Wi-Fi-based hacking tools, which it showcased at the Milipol homeland security conference. The company offers a product called WiNA-P, which enables a variety of attacks on smartphones by exploiting Wi-Fi networks. These attacks include delivering malware to extract data from apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook, and Skype, as well as phishing capabilities to steal login credentials through fake landing pages. Almenta also advertises an "Account Grabber" feature to identify iCloud or Android accounts by sending deceptive messages to targets.

Alongside WiNA-P, Almenta promotes a product called “Observer,” which offers “worldwide geo location,” as described in a blurb on Milipol’s website. A brochure for “Observer” reveals that, with only a target’s mobile phone number, the device’s location can be pinpointed and displayed on a Google Maps interface.

The company claims its tools can operate from up to 500 meters away and target as many as 50 devices simultaneously. Almenta's technology reportedly relies on tools from other Israeli surveillance firms, such as WiSpear and Jenovice, with costs for such systems starting at $1 million.
