children.text: Operation Zero is a Russian zero-day exploit brokerage operating under the legal entity Matrix LLC, owned by Sergey Sergeyevich Zelenyuk. The company has openly stated it will only sell exploits to customers in non-NATO countries, including the Russian government and foreign intelligence agencies. Beyond exploit brokering, Operation Zero has also pursued the development of spyware and tools to extract personal data from users of AI applications such as large language models.

Operation Zero came further into the spotlight when it was revealed that Peter Williams, a 39-year-old Australian national and former executive at U.S. defense contractor L3Harris, stole eight classified zero-day exploits from his employer between 2022 and 2025 and sold them to Operation Zero for millions of dollars. Operation Zero then re-sold these stolen tools, originally intended solely for the U.S. government and its allies, to unauthorized users. Williams was sentenced to over seven years in federal prison after pleading guilty.

In February 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Zelenyuk, Operation Zero / Matrix LLC, and several associates, including Azizjon Makhmudovich Mamashoyev and Oleg Vyacheslavovich Kucherov (a suspected member of the Trickbot cybercrime gang), for their role in acquiring and distributing cyber tools.

Zelenyuk also established a UAE-based technology company called STS specifically to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Russian bank accounts and to conduct business with entities in Asia and the Middle East. STS was among the entities sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury in February 2026 alongside Zelenyuk and Operation Zero.

children.text: Coruna is an iPhone hacking toolkit first identified by security researchers in February 2025. According to mobile security company iVerify and reporting by TechCrunch, the exploit kit is believed to have been created by the hacking and surveillance division of US military contractor L3Harris and developed for use by the US government.

According to Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which named the toolkit, Coruna contains five complete iOS exploit chains leveraging a total of 23 distinct vulnerabilities, targeting iPhones running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1. The kit primarily exploits Apple's WebKit browser framework, enabling "watering hole" attacks that silently compromise a device when a user simply visits a malicious website. The toolkit is estimated to have infected tens of thousands of phones worldwide.

Coruna has also proliferated beyond its original operator. Google tracked its use by a suspected Russian espionage group (UNC6353) in watering hole attacks targeting Ukrainian users, and later by a financially motivated Chinese cybercriminal operation (UNC6691) stealing cryptocurrency. The exact mechanism of proliferation remains unclear, but Google says it points to an active market for "second-hand" zero-day exploits and unscrupulous brokers facilitating the spread of nation-state-grade tools to criminals and foreign intelligence services.

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

children.text: Gamma Group is an Anglo-German technology company, founded in 1990, that sells surveillance and more specifically spyware to governments and police forces around the world. The firm operates through a network of entities, including a Munich-based arm (FinFisher GmbH) and the U.K.-linked Lench IT Solutions plc, which marketed the company's spyware through law enforcement channels.
Its best-known product, FinFisher (also marketed as FinSpy), is a remote monitoring and intrusion suite designed to give government clients covert access to targets' computers and mobile devices.

The software can be installed surreptitiously by exploiting security gaps in the update procedures of legitimate, non-suspect software, and is pitched to clients as a solution for monitoring mobile and "security-aware" targets who use encrypted communications, change location frequently, or reside abroad. Once deployed, FinSpy enables capabilities such as country tracing, remote microphone activation, and the collection of data routed through anonymizing proxy chains (FinFisher Relay and FinSpy Proxy) to disguise the operator's identity and the location of the master server.

Gamma Group's products have repeatedly been linked to human rights abuses and politically motivated targeting. Research by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab identified roughly 33 likely government users of FinFisher across 32 countries.

In 2023, following a criminal complaint by Reporters Without Borders and three other organizations, prosecutors in Munich charged four former senior representatives of the FinFisher group with illegally selling surveillance software to authoritarian governments.

children.text: PCS Security Pte Ltd (PCSS) is a Singaporean surveillance and security systems integrator that has been in operation since 1998 and is a supplier of government surveillance infrastructures in Singapore as well as internationally. Marketing materials from the company note that it has been playing a "vital role in Singapore's homeland security" for more than 25 years by entering into a Strategic Partnership for Innovation (SPI) agreement with HTX, the Singapore government agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs that develops technologies for public safety and homeland security operations.

According to the leaked WikiLeaks documents, the company was one of the clients of FinFisher, a German surveillance software provider that exploits vulnerabilities in commonly used software applications like iTunes and Microsoft Word to take control over the devices and obtain information. According to reports, PCS Security is alleged to have paid approximately €3.2 million for the use of FinFisher's spyware that works across all major operating systems including Windows, OS X, Linux, and Android.

The company also offers training on Magnet Forensics, which is a digital investigation tool that is used to extract and analyze data from computers and mobile phones, often used by government agencies for digital surveillance and data collection.
The company has close associations with Singapore government agencies and has more than 10 years of experience providing IT security solutions to government agencies.

children.text: Trovicor originated as part of Siemens' voice and data recording division. This division became part of Nokia Siemens Networks (NSN) in 2007, a joint venture between Siemens and Nokia Oyj. In March 2009, NSN sold the division, known then as Intelligence Solutions, to Perusa Partners Fund. This move was partly to disassociate NSN from the contentious surveillance industry and its extensive human rights violations. Perusa subsequently rebranded the division as Trovicor, while retaining much of the original equipment and workforce from before the sale. Trovicor’s surveillance and interception products have enabled at least one government in the Gulf to spy on and arrest journalists and dissidents. Trovicor also has a partnership with Gamma Group, developer of the notorious FinFisher spyware. In 2009, when the company was part of NSN, Trovicor sol​d surveillance technology to Iran.
The company is now known as Data Fusion.

children.text: The Intellexa Consortium is a web of holding companies and vendors for spyware and surveillance services, such as Cytrox and Nexa. The group, with companies in Greece, Ireland, North Macedonia, and Hungary, enables the proliferation of commercial spyware and surveillance technologies worldwide, including to authoritarian regimes. Each company within the Intellexa Group maintains business relationships with numerous other entities within the group, many of which incorporate the "Intellexa" name in various capacities. The group is founded and led by Tal Dilian, a former commander of an elite Israeli military intelligence unit.

Through one of its affiliated companies, Intellexa Group oversees the distribution and support of the Predator spyware service. Predator is designed to infiltrate, monitor, and extract data from targeted devices. Installation can occur through "zero-click" or "one-click" methods. In a zero-click scenario, a victim's mobile browser is covertly redirected to a malicious website. Alternatively, one-click infections involve victims unwittingly clicking on malicious links, such as those disguised as legitimate websites. Once installed, Predator enables remote access to monitor the target device, control local microphones and cameras, and extract various forms of data, including files, messages, and location information. Predator has been reportedly sold to governments with extensive records of human rights abuses.

In February 2026, a Greek court convicted four business executives linked to Intellexa, including founder Tal Dilian, his ex-wife and business partner Sara Hamou, Intellexa executive Felix Bitzios, and Yiannis Lavranos, owner of the Greek security firm that purchased Intellexa's Predator spyware, for their involvement in the illegal wiretapping of government ministers, military officials, and journalists. The four were sentenced to eight years in prison, suspended pending appeals, for breaching the confidentiality of telephone communications and illegally accessing information systems.

children.text: Tykelab, a little-known company based in Rome, has been utilizing dozens of phone networks, often located on remote Pacific islands, to send tens of thousands of secret “tracking packets” worldwide. These packets target individuals in countries such as Libya, Nicaragua, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Iraq, Mali, Greece, and Portugal, as well as within Italy itself. Tykelab exploits longstanding but often unaddressed vulnerabilities in global phone networks, allowing third parties to track phone users’ locations and potentially intercept their calls without leaving any trace on the devices. Tykelab’s parent company, RCS Lab, has also developed a powerful phone hacking tool called Hermit. Once installed on a victim’s device, Hermit can remotely activate the phone’s microphone, record calls, access messages, call logs, contacts, photos, and other sensitive data.

children.text: Advanced German Technology (AGT) is a surveillance vendor founded by two Syrian-German brothers, Anas and Aghiath Chbib. While it has a letterbox office in Berlin, Germany, its operational headquarters is in Dubai, UAE.

AGT is a provider of various surveillance technologies, offering a suite of products that includes interception, digital forensics, and social media monitoring. The company claims to serve corporations, governments, law enforcement, and intelligence agencies worldwide.

According to a Privacy International investigation, AGT enabled the construction of surveillance systems in Syria over a decade leading up to the Arab Spring. Between 2007-2012, AGT partnered with Italian-headquartered RCS to propose using US-origin equipment for a satellite internet monitoring project aimed at intercepting communications. Documents also reveal that AGT was prepared to sell probes from US firm AccessData to MTN Syria, one of the country's mobile service providers, despite US sanctions restricting such exports at the time.
Additionally, AGT was involved in surveillance operations in Libya under Muammar Gaddafi's regime.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

BadBazaar is a mobile spyware tool with variants targeting both Android and iOS devices. It has been linked to Chinese-backed hacking groups, such as APT15. This group is known by various names assigned by different cybersecurity organizations, including Vixen Panda, Ke3chang, Nickel, Playful Taurus, BackdoorDiplomacy, Mirage, GREF, RoyalAPT, Nylon Typhoon, Flea, and Red Vulture. 

BadBazaar has primarily been used to target Uyghur, Tibetan, and Taiwanese individuals, as well as civil society actors who may oppose Chinese state interests.

The spyware is distributed through trojanized apps, including fake versions of popular communication tools like Signal and Telegram, as well as apps tailored to specific communities, such as Uyghur-language Quran apps. Once installed, BadBazaar can collect sensitive data, including call logs, GPS locations, SMS messages, and files. The spyware has also been observed spreading via social media platforms and official app stores.

The Chengdu-based contractor, Sichuan Dianke Network Security Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as UPSEC), was linked to the deployment of this malware.

children.text: DarkNimbus is a cross platform spyware and remote access trojan (RAT) linked to the threat actor Earth Minotaur. First documented in 2025, it has been deployed against Uyghur and Tibetan communities after being delivered through the Moonshine exploit framework, which abuses vulnerabilities in WeChat and Chromium based applications.

Once installed, DarkNimbus enables extensive surveillance by collecting contacts, SMS messages, call logs, browser data, and messaging app conversations, while also tracking device location, recording phone calls, capturing screenshots and photos, transferring files, and executing remote commands.

Security researchers have linked the broader activity of Earth Minotaur and related Chinese state-aligned operators to targeting ethnic minority groups, human rights advocates, and individuals considered politically sensitive by Beijing.

children.text: Utimaco is a cybersecurity and compliance solutions provider that develops surveillance technology that supports data interception and retention. Their key product in this area is the Lawful Interception Management System (LIMS), which is used by law enforcement agencies to monitor and intercept communications data within a network. This system facilitates the interception of voice, data, and internet traffic, ensuring that the intercepted information can be securely transferred to law enforcement monitoring facilities.

According to the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR), Utimaco was involved in supporting a centralized surveillance system operated by Syrian Telecom, even as late as 2011 when protests against Assad's regime began. children.text: Quadream Ltd was an Israeli company that provided spyware technology primarily to government clients. The company is best known for its spyware marketed under the name “Reign”, which, like NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, reportedly utilises zero-click exploits to hack into target devices. It was founded in 2014 by a group including two former NSO Group employees, Guy Geva, and Nimrod Reznik. In 2017, a company named InReach was established in Cyprus specifically to promote Quadream products, including Reign, outside of Israel. This was arranged in order to bypass Israeli export controls. Many key employees of both InReach and Quadream have previously worked for NSO Group, Verint, and UTX Technologies.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: PenLink is a software company that develops communications surveillance and data analysis solutions for law enforcement. It has become a go-to resource for agencies monitoring users across various platforms, including Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. Its federal clients in the U.S. include the FBI and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) PenLink's flagship products, PLX and PenPoint, enable law enforcement to collect and analyze large amounts of data, including social media interactions and telecommunications records.

In 2022, PenLink acquired GeoTime, which develops data collection and analysis software, and in 2023, it acquired the Israeli surveillance company Cobwebs Technologies, which develops software that aggregates data from phones and social media, converting it into intelligence.

In October 2025, The Washington Post reported that PenLink supplied ICE with Weblocs, a cellphone location tracking system that allows the agency to monitor individuals’ movements without obtaining a court warrant.

In April 2026, the Citizen Lab published an in-depth analysis of Webloc, describing it as a global geolocation surveillance system that monitors hundreds of millions of people using data purchased from consumer apps and digital advertising. The report revealed that Webloc's customers extend well beyond ICE to include the U.S. military, multiple local police departments, and foreign governments, including Hungarian domestic intelligence and El Salvador's national police. The Citizen Lab also found that Cobwebs Technologies founder Omri Timianker, who now oversees PenLink's international operations, has links to the spyware vendor Quadream.
Review the Surveillance Watch entry for Cobwebs Technologies for more information and countries of deployment.

name: Valid

children.text: Valid is a Brazilian identity and technology company that provides facial and fingerprint biometrics, identity verification, and liveness detection, and markets these capabilities to government and law enforcement customers. Its current platform can perform automated facial matching against reference databases.

Valid has also developed facial recognition applications for law enforcement agencies. In 2025, the company described systems used by Brazilian police to identify targeted individuals in crowds, including a facial recognition deployment at a São João festival in São Luís, Maranhão, where Valid supported technology generated alerts by matching faces against databases of people.

In Paraná, Valid was contracted by the state owned IT company Celepar in 2022 to provide a system for identifying students through facial biometric recognition. The system was designed to process the biometric data of up to one million children per month, with images stored on government servers. Valid partnered with Slovak facial recognition company Innovatrics for this purpose.

In 2026, Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Paraná to halt the collection of children’s and adolescents’ biometric data for facial recognition attendance, citing inadequate legal basis, security and governance safeguards.

children.text: Speech Technology Center (STC,) also known as SpeechPro, is a Russian company that develops speech recognition, facial recognition and voice biometrics. It has its origins linked to a secretive Soviet technologies unit that operated under the KGB. According to Wired, the company's roots can be traced back to the Sharashka Marfino, a special prison for engineers and scientists during the Stalin era. In this facility, individuals plucked from various labor camps were coerced into developing technologies, including voice identification systems used for monitoring calls to foreign embassies in Moscow. According to its website, it worked with Saudi's Ministry of Interior to install an audio forensic lab in the Kingdom.

In 2019, Sberbank, the state-controlled financial powerhouse, finalized the acquisition of a 51% stake in STC. Additionally, Digital Horizon, a venture capital and business incubator firm with offices in Moscow and Tel Aviv, also secured a stake in STC.

According to the BIRN (Balkan Investigative Reporting Network) investigation into surveillance systems in Serbia, STC's voice recognition software was procured by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MUP). Serbian intermediary companies, notably AIGO and IntellSec, facilitated the supply to Serbian state institutions.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. AccessData Group was a U.S.-based cybersecurity company that developed digital forensics investigation technology. The technology was used by law enforcement agencies worldwide, including in Nigeria, where it was employed alongside other forensic tools for extracting information from seized devices.

AccessData's merger with Exterro created a powerful surveillance conglomerate. Their combined digital forensics and data extraction capabilities give law enforcement and government agencies unprecedented access to personal information, particularly given the company's two-decade history of developing tools that can crack passwords, decrypt files, and extract sensitive personal data from devices without user consent.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: MSAB is a Swedish forensic technology company. Its software, XRY, which can decrypt passwords and recover deleted data, was reportedly used by Hong Kong police in 2020 to access pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong's phone in under an hour.  Leaked documents in 2021 showed that Myanmar's military junta used MSAB's technology to extract data from phones, including deleted content. In the U.S, the San Diego Police Department employs MSAB's XRY software to extract data from mobile devices in investigations. It's also used by the FBI and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB), among other government agencies.

MSAB developed tools for CPB to gather information from vehicles at border crossings by extracting data from car infotainment systems. These systems store a wealth of information, including call logs, text messages, GPS locations, and paired device data.
MSAB's phone extraction tools were also supplied to Moroccan authorities under EU-funded border management programs to surveil migrants transiting North Africa.
Its reseller in Hong Kong is S-Tech, which also sells surveillance tools from Oxygen Forensics and BlackBag (acquired by Cellebrite in 2020.)

children.text:
Veraset is a provider of location and mobility data, offering datasets derived from GPS signals. According to the Washington Post, Veraset shared billions of phone location records with the D.C. government as part of a COVID-19 tracking effort. This data, which was provided without people's consent, was used to monitor movement patterns during the pandemic. However, officials will not disclose the specific reasons for acquiring the data or how it was used. 

Veraset was originally founded as a subsidiary of SafeGraph, but the two companies now operate independently.

children.text:
SafeGraph is a data broker known for collecting and selling aggregated location data derived from mobile apps. The company has faced significant criticism for selling data related to visits to sensitive locations, such as abortion clinics, including Planned Parenthood facilities. This data, marketed under its "Patterns" product, tracks where visitors come from, how long they stay, and where they go afterward. 

In addition to its commercial ventures, SafeGraph has expanded its operations into government and military contracts. Notably, it secured a contract with the U.S. Air Force to provide data for purposes such as analyzing human activity for military operations. The company also markets its data for monitoring "adversaries" and supporting intelligence initiatives.

SafeGraph's investors include In-Q-Tel, the VC arm of the CIA, Peter Thiel and the former head of Saudi intelligence.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

Cognyte, currently located in Herzliya, Israel, shares an address with Verint and now provides cyberintelligence services similar to those previously offered by Verint. An investigation by Haaretz uncovered that Cognyte's mass surveillance technology has been sold to Myanmar in recent years. Its software was also unlawfully utilized by Brazil’s intelligence agency to monitor and intimidate prominent politicians, journalists, judges, and environmental officials in the country during Jair Bolsonaro’s far-right administration. In 2022, Cognyte sold a portion of their intelligence analytics software to the Volaris Group, a Canadian private equity firm, for US $47.5 million.

The company also brought on Nadav Argaman, the former director of Israel’s internal security service Shin Bet, as a strategic senior advisor to continue developing closer ties to Israel’s intelligence establishment.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: PenLink is a software company that develops communications surveillance and data analysis solutions for law enforcement. It has become a go-to resource for agencies monitoring users across various platforms, including Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. Its federal clients in the U.S. include the FBI and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) PenLink's flagship products, PLX and PenPoint, enable law enforcement to collect and analyze large amounts of data, including social media interactions and telecommunications records.

In 2022, PenLink acquired GeoTime, which develops data collection and analysis software, and in 2023, it acquired the Israeli surveillance company Cobwebs Technologies, which develops software that aggregates data from phones and social media, converting it into intelligence.

In October 2025, The Washington Post reported that PenLink supplied ICE with Weblocs, a cellphone location tracking system that allows the agency to monitor individuals’ movements without obtaining a court warrant.

In April 2026, the Citizen Lab published an in-depth analysis of Webloc, describing it as a global geolocation surveillance system that monitors hundreds of millions of people using data purchased from consumer apps and digital advertising. The report revealed that Webloc's customers extend well beyond ICE to include the U.S. military, multiple local police departments, and foreign governments, including Hungarian domestic intelligence and El Salvador's national police. The Citizen Lab also found that Cobwebs Technologies founder Omri Timianker, who now oversees PenLink's international operations, has links to the spyware vendor Quadream.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

AdVantage, an advertising intelligence (AdINT) platform. Investigative reporting from El Faro found procurement documents showing the police acquired or sought to acquire the Wave Guard Tracer system through Israeli reseller EyeTech Solutions. children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: PenLink is a software company that develops communications surveillance and data analysis solutions for law enforcement. It has become a go-to resource for agencies monitoring users across various platforms, including Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. Its federal clients in the U.S. include the FBI and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE.) PenLink's flagship products, PLX and PenPoint, enable law enforcement to collect and analyze large amounts of data, including social media interactions and telecommunications records.

In 2022, PenLink acquired GeoTime, which develops data collection and analysis software, and in 2023, it acquired the Israeli surveillance company Cobwebs Technologies, which develops software that aggregates data from phones and social media, converting it into intelligence.

In October 2025, The Washington Post reported that PenLink supplied ICE with Weblocs, a cellphone location tracking system that allows the agency to monitor individuals’ movements without obtaining a court warrant.

In April 2026, the Citizen Lab published an in-depth analysis of Webloc, describing it as a global geolocation surveillance system that monitors hundreds of millions of people using data purchased from consumer apps and digital advertising. The report revealed that Webloc's customers extend well beyond ICE to include the U.S. military, multiple local police departments, and foreign governments, including Hungarian domestic intelligence and El Salvador's national police. The Citizen Lab also found that Cobwebs Technologies founder Omri Timianker, who now oversees PenLink's international operations, has links to the spyware vendor Quadream.
Review the Surveillance Watch entry for Cobwebs Technologies for more information and countries of deployment.

children.text:
Ring, acquired by Amazon in 2018 for approximately $1 billion, is a smart doorbell and security camera company that has become central to a major surveillance controversy due to its extensive partnerships with police departments across the United States. These partnerships have allowed law enforcement to request doorbell and security camera footage directly from Ring users, often without requiring a warrant. 

Ring shut down its direct police request feature in January 2024. However, the company reversed course in July 2025 by partnering with Axon to reintroduce police access to user footage through Axon's digital evidence management system.

In October 2025, Ring announced a partnership with Flock, a network of AI cameras used by law enforcement, enabling agencies to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.
A few months later, in February 2026, Ring cancelled its partnership with Flock after major backlash and campaigns by various advocacy groups.
In June 2026, Amazon was hit with a class action lawsuit filed in Seattle, alleging that Ring's "Familiar Faces" feature stores facial-recognition data of passersby without their consent.

term.definition: Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras are automated surveillance systems that use cameras and software to automatically capture, analyze, and store vehicle license plate information from passing vehicles. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

children.text: Flock Safety is a technology company that develops AI-powered surveillance systems. Its products include high definition cameras equipped with automated license plate recognition (

) technology that capture and analyze vehicles entering and exiting monitored areas, as well as AI-enabled audio detection sensors designed to identify and log vehicle data. They also feature FlockOS in their suite of products, which integrates first and third-party data from video, license plate recognition (LPR), and audio detection to provide real-time intelligence through advanced search, a customizable map and other options.
In 2024, Flock Safety acquired drone startup Aerodome for over $300 million. This acquisition allows Flock Safety to broaden its reach into autonomous police drone surveillance.

In 2025, it was revealed that the company was considering using hacked or breached data to create Nova, a surveillance tool intended for law enforcement use. That same year, a report by 404 Media revealed that a Texas police officer used Flock’s nationwide license plate camera network to track a woman who had traveled out of state to obtain an abortion.
In October 2025, Amazon's Ring announced a partnership with Flock, enabling agencies that use Flock to request Ring users to share surveillance footage.

Throughout 2025, police departments and U.S Border Patrol officials used Flock's ALPR cameras to monitor protests hundreds of times across the U.S, including No Kings protests in June and October, based on data obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In February 2026, Milwaukee police officer Josue Ayala was criminally charged for using Flock Safety's license plate recognition technology to personally surveil a person he was dating and that person's ex for two months while on duty.

An investigation found that multiple law enforcement officers across the U.S. had misused Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network to surveil romantic partners, ex-partners, neighbors, and other individuals for personal reasons.

As of August 2026, Flock was expanding its police drone surveillance business, which it described as its fastest growing line of products. The company said more than 200 police agencies and private companies were using its drone systems, which can be launched from rooftop docks and equipped with 40x optical zoom. The company's Alpha drone is also capable of reading license plates from a distance of 2,000 feet.

entity.name: Metrea

children.text: Metrea, formerly known as Meta Aerospace, is a US security and defense service provider tied to the American military and secret services. Flight tracking has revealed that Metrea flies surveillance missions for the EU border agency Frontex under a €14.5 million contract, operating at least one aircraft for the EU's migration-deterrence efforts in the western Mediterranean. Metrea did not win the contract directly: the aircraft is deployed under a 2023 framework contract for "aerial surveillance services" held by Luxembourg-based CAE Aviation, which engages Metrea as a subcontractor. This is the first known instance of a company from a non-EU state searching for migrant boats in the Mediterranean on Frontex's behalf.

The deployment came to light only through the tracking of conspicuous flight patterns resembling those of coastguards or Frontex, discovered by London-based researcher Sasha Milonova, who identified the aircraft via its ICAO hex code.

The firm also leased a Gulfstream jet, staffed by US personnel, to the British Ministry of Defence for spy missions over Gaza, taking off from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Documents obtained by Declassified UK showed the UK had contracted Metrea to fly unarmed missions over Gaza from January to February 2024.
In 2022, Metrea participated in the Catalyst Accelerator, a U.S. Department of Defense affiliated accelerator program that supports companies developing national security and defense technologies.

entity.name: Equifax

children.text: Equifax is one of the three major U.S. consumer credit reporting bureaus. Operating as a data broker, its products provide U.S. immigration authorities and law enforcement with information used to locate people targeted for arrest and deportation. Between 2005 and September 2024, the U.S Department of Homeland Security (DHS) awarded Equifax contracts worth at least $16.1 million, while total U.S. federal government contracts with the company exceeded $365 million during the same period.

ICE uses or has used multiple Equifax databases, mainly through third-party platforms like LexisNexis Accurint and Thomson Reuters CLEAR, to locate people targeted for arrest or deportation. ICE has also specifically paid for access to data from Appriss, a company Equifax owns.

Since early 2021, ICE has used a database called Justice Intelligence (formerly JusticeXchange), a product of Equifax subsidiary and data broker Appriss Insights. This system collects and makes searchable real-time incarceration release data from thousands of U.S. jails and prisons, which ICE uses to learn the release dates of individuals it targets for deportation. The agency accesses Justice Intelligence as an add-on to its LexisNexis Accurint subscription.

children.text: Cintel was a U.S. surveillance technology company that developed automated license plate recognition (ALPR), video surveillance, and intelligence systems for law enforcement agencies. The company's CLARITY platform processed license plate data, while its CAPTURE cameras were designed to capture plates at extended distances.
In Miami, Cintel operated an LPR data server used by the Miami Police Department and Miami-Dade Police Department to store, retrieve, and share license plate data among law enforcement agencies.
GovTribe records Cintel LLC receiving a 2014 FBI purchase order for mobile LPR reader kits that were to be integrated with the FBI's existing LPR data infrastructure.
Cintel was acquired by Insight LPR, with its LPR data migrated to Insight's cloud platform.

entity.name: Insight LPR

children.text: Insight LPR provides automated license plate recognition (ALPR) systems to law enforcement, neighborhoods, schools, and other organizations. Its cameras capture plates and vehicle details on an ongoing basis, then use software to cross reference that information against hotlists and send alerts when a targeted vehicle is detected. The company says its network covers more than 1,500 U.S. cities and has scanned more than 10 billion plates.

In February 2026, Insight LPR announced a partnership with LiveView Technologies, Inc. (LVT) to integrate its license plate recognition technology into LVT’s mobile surveillance units, which are used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: DataWorks Plus is a South Carolina-based company that provides advanced surveillance technology, equipping police with the ability to identify faces from surveillance footage in real time. One of their flagship products, FaceWatch Plus, offers "continuous screening and monitoring of live video streams," as described on the company's website. This technology was adopted by law enforcement agencies in cities like Chicago and Detroit, enabling real-time identification from live video feeds. Another one of their products, FaceCompare Plus, offers standalone morphological facial comparison, allowing agencies to compare two facial images side-by-side without a full facial recognition system.

The use of DataWorks Plus' technology has raised significant concerns, particularly regarding its reliability and potential for racial bias. In Detroit, the police department's use of this facial recognition technology has been criticized for its almost exclusive application against Black people in 2020. The department's own data revealed that the technology frequently misidentifies people, with Former Detroit Police Chief James Craig admitting that the system almost never brings back a direct match and often leads to incorrect identifications.

Despite these issues, DataWorks Plus does not provide specific guidance to law enforcement on how to use the software, leaving decisions largely to the discretion of individual officers. This has led to wrongful arrests and raised concerns among human rights advocates about the implications for privacy and racial justice.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: The Israeli intelligence company Cellebrite is best recognized for its flagship product, the Universal Forensic Extraction Device (UFED). This device is renowned for its capabilities: bypassing passwords and encryption to unlock mobile phones and other devices, extracting valuable data, and when used in conjunction with Cellebrite's Physical Analyzer, enabling operators to analyze data thoroughly and generate detailed reports. According to Cellebrite’s parent company, the Japanese Sun Corporation, UFED has been purchased by police, military, law enforcement agencies, and intelligence services in more than 150 countries, commanding a leading position in the global market.
A report by Amnesty International reveals that Serbian authorities have utilized Cellebrite tools to unlock the mobile phones of activists and a journalist, subsequently infecting them with malware.

The Citizen Lab, in research supported by Access Now, confirmed with high confidence that Russian authorities used Cellebrite's UFED to break into an iPhone belonging to Andrey Pivovarov, a prominent Russian activist and former political prisoner. The data extraction occurred on or around June 17, 2021, during Pivovarov's detention and notably three months after Cellebrite publicly announced it was ending sales to Russia "immediately". According to a forensic report Russian authorities provided to Pivovarov, between June 15 and July 12, 2021, the Russian Ministry of Interior (MVD) used Cellebrite's UFED 4PC device and UFED Physical Analyzer software to extract and analyze data from his devices in order to build a criminal case against him.

children.text: U.S.-Israeli company Verint provides eavesdropping equipment, including "monitoring centers" that allow for the interception, monitoring, and analysis of both targeted and mass communications across various networks. These systems are integrated into a country's communication infrastructure and are capable of intercepting phone calls and emails from millions of citizens, storing the data for analysis. Verint's technology is employed in over 75 countries and can be used for nationwide mass interception, voice identification, and data mining to build detailed profiles of individuals.

Verint sold their technology to repressive regimes worldwide, including in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, South Sudan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The technology sold to Azerbaijan was reportedly used to identify the sexual orientations of individuals through social media, leading to the targeting and arrest of LGBTQ+ individuals. In the Gulf region, Verint products have been used to gather data from social networks, contributing to the repression of dissidents for their online activities. Additionally, in Indonesia, Verint's technology has been employed to compile databases of LGBTQ+ rights activists and monitor religious minorities. The company has also sold its SS7-based tracking tool SkyLock to a government client in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Verint has been linked to surveillance operations in South Sudan, where it provided communications interception equipment and support services to the government. This arrangement required the telecommunications company Vivacell to pay Verint over $762,000 to facilitate the interception of citizens' communications, as reported by Amnesty International.
In 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in a deal valued at approximately $2 billion.

children.text: Circles was a surveillance vendor that sold telecom-network exploitation tools to government clients. Its technology operated by exploiting weaknesses in Signaling System 7 (SS7), a decades-old protocol used by mobile carriers worldwide to route calls and texts between networks. By abusing this telecom infrastructure, Circles' clients could intercept phone calls and text messages, and geolocate any mobile phone in seconds using only its phone number, without needing to install anything on the target device and without leaving any forensic signatures on the victim's phone.
Its first legal entity, CT - Circles Technologies Ltd, was registered formally in Cyprus in 2008. It has since been dissolved following voluntary liquidation.
Circles was founded by former Israeli intelligence official Tal Dilian alongside co-founders Boaz Goldman and Nadia Ropleva, with Ropleva serving as CEO from 2010 until 2017.
In 2014, Circles was acquired by US private equity firm Francisco Partners and merged with NSO Group, becoming part of one of the world's most prolific spyware conglomerates.

A June 2026 Human Rights Watch investigation revealed that Circles was granted licenses to legally export telecommunication interception systems, communications monitoring software, and other surveillance technology to countries with extensive histories of using such tools against journalists, activists, and dissidents. Clients include intelligence services, military and police bodies, regional governments, and private companies. The documents also showed licensed exports to Q Cyber Technologies and NSO Group in Israel.

children.text: Ability is a security firm based in Tel Aviv. The company develops and provides interception and decryption communication tools to security and intelligence agencies, military forces, police and homeland security services.

Its surveillance capabilities include both passive and active interception of cellular communications across GSM, CDMA, UMTS, and LTE networks, as well as satellite communication interception for systems like Thuraya, Iridium, and VSAT. Ability also offers decryption tools to break encrypted communications and geolocation technologies for tracking cellular devices, and developed the Crosscan system, a portable IMSI catcher for tracking mobile devices. Its operations span across 50 countries worldwide.
Ability cooperated with NSO Group on Pegasus and handled the network side of NSO’s operations.

children.text: Equus Technologies is an Israeli company behind an advanced spyware, known as "Lipizzan," designed to steal users' data. The company offers custom solutions for law enforcement, intelligence agencies, and national security organizations. According to Google researchers, Lipizzan is a multi-stage spyware capable of monitoring and extracting a user’s emails, SMS messages, location data, voice calls, and media files. Founded in 2014 by former Mossad member Doron Cohen, Fifth Dimension became a leading producer of surveillance technology with the backing of notable figures such as former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz, who served as the company's chairman, and former Mossad deputy head Ram Ben-Barak. The company's systems are employed to analyze large amounts of data, including social media activity, to identify potential security threats and prevent incidents before they occur. The company specializes in predictive policing tools and comprehensive data analysis, including sophisticated data processing techniques to identify patterns and correlations based on mass surveillance data. 

Fifth Dimension collaborated with the Israel Police on a project involving artificial intelligence for law enforcement purposes. This partnership, which did not go through a tender process, involved a pilot program costing about 4 million shekels ($1.1 million) and concluded in 2017. The initiative was described as a "game changer" by Police Chief Roni Alsheikh. However, Fifth Dimension ceased operations due to U.S. sanctions on one of its investors, Viktor Vekselberg, which affected its primary market in the U.S.

The company ceased operations in December 2018, after an unsuccessful acquisition bid from NSO Group. At its height, Fifth Dimension had secured $40 million in funding and employed 100 people.

children.text: Patternz is an Israeli company that builds geolocation technology derived from advertising data (ADINT) with advanced spyware capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Yoad Gidron, a former technical director at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, alongside Nimrod Schwartz and Rafi Ton of digital advertising firm NUVIAD, Patternz leverages Mobile Advertising ID (MAID) technology to track individuals' locations in real time and build comprehensive target profiles. This approach is often used to bypass the need for legal warrants and benefits from more flexible export regulations compared to traditional surveillance tools.

The company’s platform not only enables precise tracking and profiling but can also issue alerts when a target reaches specific destinations. Patternz is reportedly working on even more advanced solutions, including the integration of spyware capabilities into the ad-tech stack, potentially deploying Trojans through advertising frameworks. In January 2024, the business development firm Improvate The Future (ITF) filed a lawsuit against Patternz for alleged non-payment of services. ITF, which boasts a high-profile advisory board including former Israeli cybersecurity chief Yigal Unna and several ex-prime ministers, had previously facilitated Patternz's participation in international cyber delegations.
Udi Doenyas, Patternz’s technical director, is a former architect of NSO Group's Pegasus spyware and has been a key figure in the company’s operations.

children.text: Cyberglobes, an Israeli open-source intelligence (OSINT) firm, is an exporter of intelligence solutions despite facing bans from platforms like Facebook due to its spying activities.

Founded in 2016 by former Israeli intelligence officers Pini Kleiner and Idan Frischberg, the company has helped various government agencies, including in Nigeria, Rwanda, Mozambique, and Kuwait, to collect information on protesters, dissidents, and political activists using its software tools that scrape data from social networks and the dark web.
One of the documents revealed by a leak shows that Indonesia requested and received assistance from the company in identifying and creating lists of members of LGBT communities in the country.

Other leaked documents revealed that CyberGlobes employees actively assisted clients in identifying and locating citizens based on their political views, with one tool enabling operators to mark an area on a map and retrieve all Instagram posts from that location and timeframe. The documents also exposed CyberGlobes targeted environmental activists in Europe and North America.

Cyberglobes has a history in the Indian market, having demonstrated its solutions to Indian police forces as early as 2019. It has also been pitching its social network surveillance technologies to the United Arab Emirates.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company that develops and sells surveillance tools, most notably the Pegasus spyware, which can infiltrate mobile phones to extract messages, emails, photos, passwords, location data, and other sensitive information. The company has also been linked to Chrysaor, an Android malware sample discovered by researchers.

NSO markets its products primarily to governments and law enforcement agencies, and its spyware has been repeatedly found on the devices of journalists, activists, political dissidents, and human rights defenders. Research by organizations such as Citizen Lab has documented Pegasus deployments against individuals targeted by governments with records of repressing civil society and opposition groups.

NSO Group has operated under several corporate names, including Q Cyber Technologies in Israel and OSY Technologies in Luxembourg, with a North American subsidiary known as WestBridge Technologies. In 2019, London-based private equity firm Novalpina Capital acquired NSO in a deal reportedly valued at around $1 billion. In 2023, Luxembourg based Dufresne Holdings became the company’s owner. In December 2024, a U.S. judge found NSO Group liable for hacking in a lawsuit brought by Meta Platforms over Pegasus targeting of WhatsApp users.

In 2025, a U.S. jury ordered NSO to pay approximately $167 million in damages to WhatsApp, including punitive damages, in what became one of the largest legal penalties against a commercial spyware company.
In October 2025, it was revealed that a group of U.S. investors led by Hollywood producer Robert Simonds is acquiring the company.

children.text: WebDetetive is a Brazilian commercial spyware and stalkerware platform designed to secretly monitor Android devices. It has been marketed as a parental control and device monitoring tool but provides invasive surveillance capabilities, including access to messages, call logs, contacts, device location, photos, and other sensitive data. WebDetetive appears to have emerged as a localized Brazilian offshoot or rebranding of the OwnSpy platform.

In 2023, WebDetetive suffered a major data breach that exposed internal company data and customer information, including credentials and data linked to monitored devices. Security researchers reported that the breach revealed the scale of the platform’s surveillance operations and highlighted the risks posed by commercial spyware services that enable covert tracking of individuals without their knowledge or consent.

children.text: Mobile Innovations is a Spanish company based in Madrid and the parent behind the OwnSpy consumer stalkerware product. Beyond OwnSpy, the company has operated a family of related mobile tracking and spoofing apps, including iLocalis, iGotYa, and FakeLocation.

The company's most well known app, OwnSpy, is stalkerware that is covertly installed on a target's device and streams its contents (messages, calls, photos, and location) to a dashboard viewable by whoever planted it. Unlike most phone monitoring apps, OwnSpy does not simply hide from the home screen but disguises itself as an Android system Wi-Fi app.

Investigative reporting found that the Brazil based WebDetetive was effectively a repackaged copy of OwnSpy's spyware, built on a commission model in which third parties promote the app and OwnSpy takes a cut. Independent research has concluded that reseller sites such as WebDetetive and SaferSpy are most likely operated in large part by Mobile Innovations itself, citing shared infrastructure and near simultaneous vulnerability fixes across those sites.

In July 2022, WhatsApp sued Mobile Innovations and its founder Antonio José Calatrava Pérez in a Madrid commercial court, alleging that OwnSpy and a related app, Wossip, infringed WhatsApp's IP rights, constituted unfair competition, and violated its terms of use by capturing users' messages, calls, status, online activity, and profile data. The parties settled: Mobile Innovations agreed to cease and desist from developing or operating Wossip and to delete all copies, to strip OwnSpy of all functionality targeting WhatsApp and other Meta platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Oculus), to stop using the associated trademarks, and to pay a monetary penalty.

children.text: Cobwebs Technologies is an Israeli company whose surveillance software collects data from phones and social media activity. Its product portfolio includes Tangles, a web and social media monitoring platform, and Webloc, an ad-based geolocation surveillance system that monitors data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices globally, using information purchased from consumer apps and digital advertising. Cobwebs also developed Lynx, a tool for managing fake online identities, and Trapdoor, a social engineering platform that the Citizen Lab assesses can help facilitate the deployment of malware.
Cobwebs founder Omri Timianker has links to the spyware vendor Quadream and now oversees Penlink's international operations.
Cobwebs has secured contracts with several U.S federal agencies, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through its Delaware-based branch, Cobwebs America Inc.

In 2023, Cobwebs was acquired by U.S. investment firm Spire Capital and merged with Penlink, a U.S.-based surveillance technology vendor also owned by Spire Capital. The three Cobwebs founders have since taken over key executive roles at Penlink. Cobwebs' Israeli, U.K., and German entities were rebranded under the Penlink name.

U.S. customers of Webloc and Tangles include ICE, the U.S. military, Texas Department of Public Safety, DHS West Virginia, NYC district attorneys, and police departments in Los Angeles, Dallas, Baltimore, Tucson, Durham, and smaller jurisdictions. International users include Hungarian domestic intelligence (since at least 2022) and the national police in El Salvador.
